Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)2164 words
Four childhood recommendations

Four recommendations are given: community programmes, playgrounds and Play Values Framework, screen-time guidance and safeguards, and whole-of-Government coordination.

covers 18 highlighted sentences in 10 sections · also: Childhood and long-term government thinking, Childhood as free stage, Excessive screen use harms
[+2 sentences]Mr Speaker, at my introduction at Bukit Canberra last year, I spoke about healthy minds and healthy bodies for our children. Today, I want to return to that idea, starting with screen-free children.
Childhood, below the age of 18, is the one stage of life where children should be free. Free to play, free to wonder, free to make mistakes, and free from unnecessary pressures and anxieties.
[+21 sentences] Increasingly, that means being screen-free too. Not because screens are inherently bad, but because childhood development requires experiences that no screen can fully replicate. This Adjournment Motion is not about opposing screens as tools for education or communication. Rather, it is about ensuring that children have meaningful alternatives to screens, and that those alternatives remain affordable and accessible to every family. Our television at home broke down when my first child was born and we never replaced it. Friends and volunteers who visit are still caught off guard by a living room with no TV console. Today, my three children use screens purposefully to video call their grandparents, to watch a science experiment before trying it themselves or to find song lyrics so that we can sing together. Screens are tools, not companions. We got lucky with a broken television. I know how easy it is to hand a child a screen and buy yourself 20 minutes to shower or simply catch your breath. For families who have less time, less space and fewer alternatives, the screen might feel like the only option. This is what brings me to this Motion today. In my maiden speech, I said that Singapore is what it is today because we invested heavily in human capital, our only enduring competitive advantage. Yet, some of the foundations of human capital are built much earlier through play, social interaction, curiosity and resilience. As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly capable of processing information, the qualities that make us distinctly human – empathy, curiosity, judgement and resilience – will matter even more. Watching my children as they grow, I have noticed this. The moments they were the most alive, most curious and most connected to each other and to me were never in front of a screen. They were in the playground, in conversations, in disagreements and in laughters. But screens are crowding out these experiences that were developing the very human qualities in them. You do not need to look far to see this. In coffee shops, parents and children can be sharing a meal yet entirely apart on their screens.
Research globally and in Singapore similarly links excessive screen use with poorer physical activity, weaker social interaction, behavioural challenges and poorer mental wellness.
[+10 sentences] This speech is about reclaiming childhood in the AI era. It takes a kampong to raise a child and reclaiming childhood will likewise require a whole-of-Government effort. My recommendations today span the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY), the Ministry of National Development (MND), the Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI) and the Ministry of Health (MOH) because no single Ministry can solve this challenge alone. Mr Speaker, every hour spent on a screen has an opportunity cost. It is an hour not spent running, climbing, reading, exploring, creating or interacting with others. The concern moves beyond what children are consuming online to what they are no longer doing because of screens. If we are serious about reducing children's screen dependency, we must focus not only on restrictions but also on replacements. This is not about asking the Government to choose between regulation and alternatives. We need both. Regulation reduces harm while community, play and family support create meaningful alternatives to screens.
Together, they give our children the opportunity to reclaim childhood. I have four recommendations: first, strengthen community programmes as meaningful alternatives to screens; second, improve our playgrounds and apply the Play Values Framework more broadly, recognising playgrounds as developmental infrastructure; third, strengthen screen-time guidance, engagement and social media safeguards for children below 18; and fourth, strengthen whole-of-Government coordination on childhood development.
[+11 sentences] My first recommendation is for MCCY to strengthen community programmes to support young parents who are often stretched for time. Over the past year, we piloted three initiatives in Naval Base that illustrate what this could look like. The first is Sembawang Budding Rangers. This is a child-centred outdoor learning and nature exploration programme run by our Youth Network. Following the forest school methodology, children come together for three hours every fortnight to “touch grass”. One participant, five-year-old Jingyi, developed a much deeper appreciation for nature after just two sessions. During one of them, she saw a dead bird and told her father that, “She didn’t like to see the dead bird in the forest, she felt very sad”. When her father told her that forests may be cleared for housing in Singapore, she was upset and full of questions. She has now taken it upon herself to tell her classmates not to waste paper because she explains, “Otherwise, we have to chop more trees”. She is five. No app taught her to grieve for a bird, or to connect that grief to a bigger picture or to try to change the behaviour of the people around her.
The second programme is LumiPals, a 10-week programme developing social and creative skills among children aged four to six.
[+9 sentences] Parents have noticed greater curiosity, confidence and willingness to speak up, exactly the qualities they worry are diminishing in today's digital environment. The third initiative is our "Stop the Scrolls, Start the Talks" conversation cards. Sometimes, the answer is not another app. Sometimes, it is simply a conversation. We launched the cards with two local eateries in Sembawang to encourage families to reconnect over meals, and the early response has been encouraging. These initiatives are not meant to replace parents. They are meant to support parents. Mr Speaker, I believe MCCY, working through the People's Association (PA) and community partners, has an important role in seeding and expanding regular programmes, such as Budding Rangers and LumiPals, across Singapore. This should be a concerted effort to engage children weekly and not restricted to school holidays, such as the current PA Kiddies programmes.
We introduced these programmes because many parents have told us that while resources and ideas exist online, they often lack the time, confidence or support to organise such activities themselves. Such programmes also already exist privately, some would say, but outdoor programmes can cost anywhere between $250 and $800 per child.
[+5 sentences] Meaningful alternatives to screens should not depend solely on a family's ability to pay. Existing community programmes are helpful but there is scope to make them more coordinated, visible and responsive to these young families’ needs. Therefore, I hope to see a holistic review of our community programmes for young children in Singapore, including making more affordable outdoor and tactile play programmes in the community available. Community centres, grassroots organisations and local partners are well placed to provide these meaningful alternatives to screens within every neighbourhood. My second recommendation is to continue improving our playgrounds and neighbourhood play spaces.
With around 72% of Singapore's playgrounds located within Housing and Development Board (HDB) estates, I welcome HDB's Play Values Framework, which recognises the developmental importance of play.
[+10 sentences] As the framework is progressively implemented, I hope the Government will continue to strengthen play value alongside established safety benchmarks, expand mixed age group playgrounds where practical, and incorporate more open and flexible play spaces into future estate designs. Not all play requires equipment. Some of my fondest childhood memories growing up in Yishun came from an open field outside Block 137. All I needed was a ball and some room to run. In a densely planned city, these simple spaces are becoming increasingly precious. Playgrounds and open spaces are developmental infrastructure. If we want our children off screens and outdoors, we must give them somewhere worth going. My third recommendation is for MOH and MDDI to strengthen screen time guidelines and social media regulation. Sir, there is no lack of literature today on the harms associated with excessive screen and social media use among children. Much of it reinforces what our existing screen use guidance already recognises.
An MOH-convened expert panel also found that one in three social media users aged 15 to 17 already spend more than three hours a day on social media.
[+1 sentence] This brings us back to the opportunity cost I spoke about earlier.
What else could those hours have been spent doing? I welcome Minister Josephine Teo's announcement last month that legislation will be introduced early next year to require stronger safeguards for teen users, potentially including daily time limits, restrictions on direct messaging, autoplay and infinite scroll.
[+2 sentences] I also welcome the Government's willingness to raise the minimum age of access to 18, where platforms are unable or unwilling to provide adequate safeguards. A recent development in the US is instructive.
In August, Meta reached a landmark settlement of up to US$17 billion with US states over allegations concerning the impact of its platforms on young users.
[+24 sentences] Meta agreed to introduce safeguards, including daily time limits, nighttime restrictions, stronger age assurance and restrictions on certain engagement features for users under 18. Interestingly, some of the tougher safeguards will apply only if other major platforms adopt comparable measures. Meta's argument is simple – if restrictions apply to only one platform, young users may simply migrate to another. This raises three questions for MDDI. First, will these safeguards apply consistently across designated social media services so that use does not simply migrate from one platform to another? Second, how will child development expertise inform the design of these safeguards? Third, how will MDDI assess whether the measures are actually reducing problematic social media use rather than merely achieving platform compliance? I welcome the Government's measured and targeted approach and recognise that no single intervention will solve the problem. But measured should not mean slow. Technology evolves rapidly, and our safeguards must focus not merely on compliance but outcomes and be capable of keeping pace. Mr Speaker, regulation alone cannot reclaim childhood. But without a healthier digital environment, our efforts in families, communities and neighbourhoods will always be fighting an uphill battle. That is why I hope MDDI will continue to move decisively in strengthening safeguards for our children. My fourth and final recommendation is to strengthen whole-of-Government coordination on childhood development through a National Childhood Framework. Grow Well SG, launched by MOH, MOE and MSF, is a meaningful multi-Ministry initiative to coordinate the health and development of our children. I commend the Ministries for this initiative. But Grow Well SG, for all its strengths, is primarily a health promotion strategy. Childhood, however, extends beyond health. It also encompasses play, nature, community, family relationships and increasingly, the digital environment in which our children are growing up. Countries, such as Finland, Australia and New Zealand, have developed broader frameworks for child well-being. In this vein, I urge the Government to consider expanding the Grow Well SG framework into a broader National Childhood Framework. The framework could bring together the work of MCCY, MND, MDDI, MOE, MOH and MSF under a shared vision for childhood development. It should articulate the experiences that every child in Singapore should have access to, regardless of postal code or household income, and provide a long-term roadmap towards that vision. Mr Speaker, Singapore plans decades ahead for our economy, our infrastructure, our healthcare system and our defence.
If human capital remains Singapore's greatest competitive advantage, then childhood deserves the same quality of long-term, cross-Government thinking.
[+8 sentences] Grow Well SG provides a strong foundation. A National Childhood Framework could become the next step in that journey. Mr Speaker, I began this speech with a broken television, but it healed my children’s childhood. I did not plan for it but I have come to believe it was one of the best things that happened to my family. I think about Jingyi, who grieved for a bird that she had never met and went home to tell her classmates to stop wasting paper. She is only but five years old, and she already understands that the world outside the screen is richer and worthwhile protecting. I think about the children of LumiPals, who started to speak up louder, clearer and more confidently. They are simply children, given the opportunity to do what children have always done – to grow, connect and surprise us.
Today, I have argued that reducing screen dependency requires meaningful alternatives. Regulation reduces harm, while community programmes, play-friendly neighbourhoods and family support create healthier choices.
[+2 sentences] Taken together, they help reclaim childhood. If human capital remains Singapore's greatest competitive advantage, then childhood is where that investment begins.
Our children will grow up as digital natives and screens will remain important tools, but they should never become their companions. Reclaiming childhood will require heavy coordination across Government because no single Ministry can do it alone.
[+2 sentences] It is no child's play. It is an investment in Singapore's future.

PA and Screen Smart programmes

PA has rolled out Family PLAYGround programmes, and the Screen Smart from the Start campaign has a portal with resources, digital parenting programmes and community activities.

covers 8 highlighted sentences in 4 sections · also: Government commitment to children, Grow Well SG holistic approach, Screen time guidelines and social media regulations
[+13 sentences]Mr Speaker, I thank the Member, Mr Ng Shi Xuan for his speech and in particular, for sharing his personal experiences and reflection. I think his story about the broken television and the story about little Jingyi give us some things to think about. I understand that many parents especially are very concerned about the impact of social media, of digital technology, of AI and screen time on their children. And this is also something that we as a Government are concerned about. I know they think about this; they talk about this; and they feel that more should be done. And Mr Ng Shi Xuan earlier gave four recommendations for us to look at. Actually, all of them are things that we are in agreement with; we are in alignment with. In fact, they are very aligned to the efforts that the Government has already been working on. And in fact, Mr Ng also made references to some of this in his speech. First, he made a recommendation in relation to strengthening of community programmes and to provide alternatives to screen times for the children. We are in agreement with this. We do feel that it is important to have a lot more community programmes, so that parents have alternatives that they can bring their children to. In this regard, we have actually been building on our efforts with PA.
PA has rolled out the PA Family PLAYGround  programmes.
[+1 sentence] The National Family Festival is also quite alive and translating into a lot of activities in the community, all intended to bring meaningful family bonding activities for families.
And so, this is something we can definitely scale and look into. We also have the "Screen Smart from the Start" campaign and in this, we have the bescreensmart.gov.sg portal, where we actually have resources for parents, there are digital parenting programmes, and also a lot of activities in the community that you can look out for – in the libraries, HPB programmes.
[+8 sentences] So, these are things that we can build on. I am happy to hear that Mr Ng himself has programmes in Naval Base – the Sembawang Budding Rangers, LumiPals, and the "Stop the Scrolls, Start the Talks" conversation cards. I think these are good things that we can definitely build into some of the existing efforts and scale them and have more presence in the community. The second recommendation he makes is about improving the playgrounds. We agree that physical environment is very important. It matters, and this is the feedback we will take back. But we are actually already working with different agencies and Ministries to improve access, for families to have easier access to playgrounds and also other family-friendly spaces, like parks and sports facilities. So, this is something that is already in the works.
Third, Mr Ng suggested we strengthen screen time guidelines as well as our social media regulations. He is already aware that MOH and MDDI are already working together in looking at the impact of social media on the mental health of young people.
[+7 sentences] We are already working with social media platforms to strengthen some of these safeguards. We have been answering a few Parliamentary Questions this Sitting on how we are doing it. We have already indicated our broad framework and how we will be approaching this matter. When we have more information and it is better cooked, we will inform you. We will keep the public updated about the developments on this matter. The fourth proposal that he made is for a national childhood framework. We note his proposal to study some of the frameworks that are already being done in other countries.
Actually, Grow Well SG is something that we look at as a holistic approach.
[+6 sentences] It is something that we look at holistically. We do learn lessons from other jurisdictions and contextualise it for Singapore's needs. We are working with different Ministries. These are some things that we will continue to build on and enhance. We will take his feedback, take it back and see how we will continue to improve on these efforts. But indeed, the whole intent of Grow Well SG is to have it holistic, child-centric and have multiple Ministries and a whole-of-Government approach towards looking at a child's development holistically.
I just want to assure Member that this is an effort that the Government will continue to be committed to look at. We are committed to helping children grow to be healthy, confident and resilient, especially in this digital and increasingly AI-driven world.
[+4 sentences] We will take a multi-Ministry, whole-of-Government and whole-of-society approach. Everybody has a role to play in this. We certainly look forward to continue working with the community and advisors and Members, like Mr Ng, to continue enhance the work that we are already doing. Adjourned accordingly at 5.21 pm.

Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)1740 words
Political salaries and benchmark update

Political salaries were not adjusted for 15 years since a 2011 downward restructuring, and the Committee recommends updating the MR4 benchmark from $1.1 million to $1.8 million.

covers 12 highlighted sentences in 7 sections · also: Benchmark movement and income growth, Benchmark versus paycheck and salary range, Immediate 9% adjustment and future movements
[+14 sentences]Mr Speaker, I rise to speak on the Government's response to the recommendations of the Committee reviewing the salaries of political office holders. But as a labour Member of Parliament (MP), I want to begin with what I have been hearing from our workers. The reaction on the ground is not a comfortable one. Before this debate, I ask our union leaders to speak candidly to workers in the land transport sector, our taxi and Private Hire Vehicle (PHV) drivers, bus and rail workers, and ask them what they thought. One worker put it very simply to us in Mandarin: "不是要同甘共苦吗，怎么选这个时机？" Are we not supposed to share the good times and the difficult times together? Why choose this time? I thought that question captured something very important. It was not simply a question about salary adjustments. It was a question about timing and about whether workers feel that we are sharing the same realities that they are experiencing. Some workers told us that while Singapore's economic numbers may look healthy, that is not necessarily how the economy feels to them on the ground. Workers' wages have gone up but so have their everyday expenses. Some told us that after accounting for the higher cost of living, they do not feel substantially better off, even with the support that the Government has provided. Workers worry about jobs, about business conditions, and about what restructuring and artificial intelligence (AI) may mean for their livelihoods, and against that backdrop they ask, why now? Others told us that public service should fundamentally be motivated by a desire to serve and ask why further increases were necessary when political salaries are already at levels they consider substantive.
Some could understand salaries being reviewed and adjusted, but felt that 9% was too high, instinctively comparing it with their own annual increments, which are considerably lower.
[+24 sentences] And some ask another interesting question: why wait so long so many years between the adjustments? Would it not be better to review salaries more regularly rather than wait ten or fifteen years and have a much larger headline number? These are sentiments we must take seriously. I understand them not only because workers tell me so. I understand them because I sit at the tables where their wages are negotiated. Mr Speaker, as a unionist, I have sat across the table from employers negotiating collective agreements, annual increments and bonuses. In many of the collective agreements I have worked on, annual increments are lower than 9%. I see the same realities in our progressive wage negotiations. I chair the tripartite Progressive Wage Model (PWM) clusters for food services and retail. Every increase has to be carefully worked through among unions, employers and Government, balancing our ambition to uplift workers with productivity, sector conditions and what businesses can sustain. So, I know how hard-won wage progression can be and how closely workers watch their wages, because every improvement matters to them and their families. That is why I understand the immediate reaction when workers see up to 9% – and I do not dismiss it. But there is something else that my experience negotiating wages have taught me. When we negotiate wages, we never look only at the headline number. We ask what sits behind that number. What is the benchmark? How does the pay move? What are the economic and manpower conditions? What can be sustained and what outcomes are we rewarding? These are questions we ask when negotiating a collective agreement for our transport workers or working through progressive wages for our lower-wage workers. So, these are also the questions I asked when I looked at the review. First, what does the 9% actually represent? I understand why workers instinctively compare it with their own annual increment, but they are not quite the same comparison. Workers' annual increments are part of regular wage progression and accumulate year after year.
Political salaries, by contrast, have not been adjusted for 15 years and importantly, that period begin not with an increase, but with a substantial downward restructuring in 2011.
[+1 sentence] The annual salary of an entry level MR4 Minister was reduced by 37%, but that does not by itself justify any particular adjustments today, nor does it tell us that 9% is the right number, but it does tell us that we should look at the whole period than just one number in isolation.
The Committee has now recommended that the MR4 reference benchmark be updated from $1.1 million to $1.8 million.
[+3 sentences] That is a significant movement in the benchmark. I also understand why workers will look at that number and ask questions. But here too, the time period matters.
Spread over the 15 years since 2011, the movement in the benchmark works out to be about 3.6% a year.
[+1 sentence] Over the same period, wages grew about 4.3% a year for the median worker pegged at P50, and 4.6% a year at P20 which represents workers at the lower-end of the wage distribution.
Put it another way, since the 2012 review, incomes of Singapore Citizen earners have risen by about 80% at the median and 87% at P20.
[+9 sentences] And that progress has not simply been a story of annual increments. Over these years, to sustain tripartite efforts, unions, employers and Government have worked to reshape wages and work through progressive wages, skills and career ladders, stronger links between wages, productivity, responsibilities and outcomes, and better employability for our senior and vulnerable workers. We have strengthened support for lower-wage workers through Workfare, given platform workers, formal recognition and stronger protections, and strengthened workplace fairness through legislation. These changes did not happen by accident. They reflect years of tripartite work to help our workers earn better wages, stay employable, be better protected and have a share in Singapore's progress. Of course, these percentages translate into very different dollars at different salary levels, but taken over the same period, they give us a more meaningful context for understanding how wages have moved over time. Mr Speaker, the 9% is only one number workers are looking at. That is also the benchmark itself. Here again, our experience in the Labour Movement is useful.
In wage-setting, a benchmark is not the same as your paycheck. It is a reference point within a salary structure, and under the revised framework, Ministers can be paid within a range of 75% to 125% of the reference salary for their grade.
[+3 sentences] So, I think it is important to explain plainly what the benchmark means. It does not mean that every MR4 Minister will now be paid that amount, nor is it a target salary that every Minister will eventually receive. The Government has decided not to move existing Ministers immediately to the new benchmark.
The immediate adjustment is up to 9% and there will not be further special adjustments simply to close the gap. Subsequent salary movements will depend on, rightfully, performance and responsibilities.
[+15 sentences] Mr Speaker, that distinction matters. But the benchmark must still have a credible basis and Singaporeans are entitled to scrutinise it. Mr Speaker, this brings me to what, for me, as a unionist is the heart of the matter. A wage framework does not make a number right simply because a formula exists. What matters is that there is a credible basis behind it. We know this from our work in the Labour Movement. Sometimes, we bargain hard over what may look like a small difference, because behind every percentage point is somebody's livelihood. Political service, of course, is not the same as an ordinary job. And government is not a business. So, the considerations cannot be identical, but I believe that the same discipline must apply: the basis must be clear; the framework transparent and movements in actual pay must be explainable. There is also something we should learn from the long gap between reviews. Regular review does not mean regular increase. Depending on circumstances, a review can result in an increase, no increase, or even restraint. But reviewing the framework regularly means that when salaries move or do not move, Singaporeans can understand why. There is also one other part of the framework that matters to me from a labour perspective.
Part of the political remuneration is linked to how Singapore and Singaporeans are doing: whether people have jobs and whether their real incomes are growing, whether Singaporeans lives are improving, and that Singaporeans are able to realise their dreams and aspirations.
[+9 sentences] I think that that is important. If political remuneration is tied to Singapore's progress, then our workers' progress must be part of that picture. Mr Speaker, the Prime Minister and Minister Chan have set out the Government's basis for the review earlier. I do not intend to repeat their explanations. My responsibility is to consider those explanations through the same lens I bring to wage negotiations and I ask myself a simple question, "Can I explain the basis for this outcome clearly to our workers?" I also agree with workers on one fundamental point. Political service must ultimately be motivated by a desire to serve. No salary framework can create that motivation and no salary level can substitute for it, but service and a proper remuneration framework are not contradictory. Mr Speaker, I begin with the worker who asked, "不是要同甘共苦吗？" For our workers, "同甘共苦" is something they must be able to experience and feel in their wages, their jobs, their prospects and in knowing that we are all moving forward together, through bad times and good.
It is right that we scrutinise the numbers, the benchmarks and the wage framework. We should not lose sight of why we have this framework in the first place – to enable capable people to step forward to serve, and together with every Singaporean to build a better tomorrow.
[+5 sentences] And that work continues long after this debate has concluded. As a labour MP and unionist, I will go back to the negotiating table tomorrow, pushing for better wages, better jobs, better livelihoods, better protection for our workers. And like every Member in this House, I will go back to my community and my constituents this evening to listen to serve and to continue building that future together. Because ultimately that is what "同甘共苦" means to me – through good times and bad, we will remain in this together. Mr Speaker, it is with this responsibility in mind that I support the Government's response to the review.

Variable pay and bonus disclosure

The 2012 framework contemplated up to 13.5 months of bonus, and actual variable payments to Cabinet Ministers from 2013 to 2017 averaged 9.7 months.

covers 20 highlighted sentences in 8 sections · also: Allowances last updated 2007, Committee's proposed salary increases, Mayor pay study recommendation
[+13 sentences]Mr Speaker, I refer to the Prime Minister's Ministerial Statement of two days ago on the 2026 Review of Salaries for Political Appointment Holders and Members of Parliament. I will make a few points. First, I will reflect on the 2026 Committee's report and the Government's response to it, including some observations on the challenge of attracting private sector leaders into politics. Second, I will speak about the gap between the norm annual salary for Ministers, which is used as a key reference point in the Committee's report and the total renumeration actually received by Ministers in practice. Third, I will speak about the reality of being a Workers' Party (WP) candidate and how this intersects with MP's allowance in response to the Prime Minister's point about attracting good candidates into politics. Fourth, I will speak about the job scope of Mayors in view of the inclusion in the Committee's report. And finally, I will ask why the renumeration for legislative assistants and secretarial assistants to Members of Parliament have not been reviewed. At the outset and as established by the WP in 2012, our position on political salaries is aligned with the three broad principles affirmed by the committee: (a) that political salaries should be competitive enough to attract people of the necessary calibre; (b) that political service is a calling, with its own ethos; and (c) that political renumeration should be transparent. Like in 2012, the point of divergence is on the formula that the Committee has adopted in its report. The WP favours the one it laid out in Parliament in 2012, which, in our view, went further to address the overly emotive elements surrounding discussions on political salaries by pegging it to a more accessible reference point for the public. On this point, our view remains unchanged. We take the view that pegging Ministerial salaries to a multiple of an MP's salary, which is in turn derived from a public sector appointee's salary, is preferred to one that bases Ministerial salaries from a discount to the median salary of the top 1,000 earners in Singapore. Under our 2012 proposal and with the passage of time, the increases to a Minister's total salary would be more modest.
The Government chose not to increase political salaries in both 2017 and 2023, aware of the public sensitivities of doing so. It has been about 15 years since salaries for Ministers and Members of Parliament were reviewed.
[+14 sentences] To that end, the Prime Minister's response to the Committee's recommendations reveals that the Government accepts the salary increases in full for all political appointment holders, including Members of Parliament. However, in the case of Ministers, a more calibrated and measured approach has been taken by the Prime Minister, in response to the Committee's recommendations. At its core, one of the perennial challenges in Singapore, as framed by the Prime Minister, with regard to political salaries, is determining what would be the appropriate renumeration to attract high quality private sector individuals to join political leadership as Ministers. From the evidence so far however, only a small handful have taken the plunge. The majority of Ministers continue to be sourced from the public sector. For some, it can be said that joining the Government as Ministers from the public sector potentially opens the door to a wage increase from the salary they previously earned in the Civil Service, a reality that is often overlooked when the focus is on ensuring that individuals drawn from the private sector can receive a competitive salary as Ministers. Even so, the issue does beg the question of whether it is the salary or the reality of political service today that dissuades many high-earning private sector individuals from joining politics. For some, it would not be out of order to suggest that no amount of money will persuade them to trade their suits and ties for grassroots activities and to immerse themselves in municipal concerns and the rough and tumble of politics, since all Ministers must first be elected as MPs. By the same token, I believe this House would agree with me when I say that Singaporeans would not be well-served by any individual who winces at undertaking political groundwork even if he or she is a corporate titan or a private sector high-flyer. For public service is indeed a calling with its own ethos and with deep meaning and purpose for those who immerse themselves in it. The Committee has referenced its recommendations to wage increases for Singaporeans at the 50th and 20th percentiles of incomes since 2012. This is arguably a plausible and useful comparison to consider. But employing the same reasoning to adjust the MR4 Minister's total annual salary norm produces a much more significant absolute quantum of increase. This increase has not gone unnoticed by members of the public, and it is an increase which the Committee itself considers significant.
Under the proposals in the Committee's report, the annual MP allowance package will increase from $192,500 to $259,000, an increase explained largely by inflation.
[+1 sentence] For comparison, the 2012 framework set the annual MP allowance at 17.5% of the MR4 Minister benchmark, or $192,500, which was marginally less than what MPs used to be paid before 2011.
An entry-level Minister's annual reference salary, on the other hand, will increase from $1.1 million to $1.8 million dollars under the Committee's proposal.
[+2 sentences] To be clear, a Minister also earns an MP's allowance. In percentage terms, the proposed in the MR4 Minister reference salary is about 64%, compared with about 35% for an MP.
In other words, the percentage increase for an MR4 Minister is roughly 1.8 times that of an MP. That could explain why the Prime Minister has proposed a first-step increase of up to 9% and has committed that paying a Minister $1.8 million as laid out in the committee's report is not a target.
[+1 sentence] The WP agrees with this more sober approach to raising Ministerial salaries, compared to the Committee's recommendation and notwithstanding the WP's differing position on how the underlying figure is derived.
The Prime Minister has also said that by the end of this term of Government, he expects most Ministers who remain at MR4 to be at the lower-end of the new salary range, at about $1.35 million.
[+3 sentences] I would like to clarify with the Prime Minister whether this means that after the initial adjustment of up to 9%, there will be no further general or across the board adjustment, and that any subsequent increases will be based solely on individual performance and responsibilities? Onto my second point. There appears to be some public confusion about the variable component of the MR4 Minister's total salary norm as expressed in the Committee's report.
At $1.1 million dollars today, the MR4 reference annual salary assumes 13 months of fixed pay and seven months of variable pay.
[+4 sentences] The variable components comprise the annual variable component, performance bonus and National Bonus. The Government has clarified that the $1.1 million is an all-in reference figure comprising fixed and variable components. A Mothership post on Tuesday reported that the bonus component was "up to" seven months in total a year, taking reference from the norm annual salary for Ministers. This is correct.
However, we know that the 2012 framework for political salaries contemplated variable components, or a total bonus of up to 13.5 months a year, with the actual amount depending on the annual variable component, performance bonus and the National Bonus. We also know that the Government disclosed that from 2013 to 2017, actual variable payments of the bonus to Cabinet Ministers averaged 9.7 months a year, not seven months as assumed by the annual salary norm in the Committee's report. In Parliament in February this year, WP's Non-Constituency Member of Parliament Eileen Chong asked for the ranges of performance bonus, National Bonus and annual variable component received by Ministers from 2018 to 2024. She did not receive a helpful reply from the Government, with only a range provided for the annual variable component at 0 to 1.5 months.
[+15 sentences] That being the case, would it not be useful for the purposes of transparency, which is a principle this House agrees to with regard to political salaries, to disclose how actual total remuneration received by MR4 Ministers has compared with the annual salary norm since the new formula was introduced in 2012? This would provide a more accurate picture of what Ministers have actually received in practice, as distinct from the annual total salary norm used by the Committee as a key point of reference. In conjunction with this point, the Committee's proposal calls for a wider range of salaries at each Ministerial grade to accommodate a greater diversity of talent. While potentially giving the People's Action Party (PAP) more flexibility in recruiting political candidates from the private sector, as alluded to by the Prime Minister, I would caution that this increased flexibility will also contribute to a concomitant increase in public scrutiny about the total annual salaries of individual Ministers in concert with the principle that salaries ought to be transparent. It would follow that this information should be published accordingly in a practical format that promotes public understanding of the total salaries earned by Ministers. Onto my third point. The Prime Minister observed in his Ministerial Statement that a proper MP allowance would enable both the PAP and the WP to recruit and field strong candidates. I note the Prime Minister's view that the presence of the Opposition has resulted in a higher quality of debate in this House. This is good for Singapore as Parliament is an important platform to ventilate different views and for the Opposition to serve as an effective check and balance on the Government. However, at this point in our nation's political history, in my view, the raison d'etre of both the WP and the PAP is very different. Simply put, a sufficient MP allowance is not a reason Singaporeans choose to stand on the WP ticket and remuneration is not the device or platform through which the WP attracts candidates or can attract candidates. The point I wish to make is not that the MP remuneration is unimportant, it is that remuneration is not what drives an individual Singaporean to become a WP candidate. The WP fields candidates who not only believe in a more democratic and balanced political system, but they are prepared to stand behind their convictions against significant odds while working for Singaporeans on the ground. The reality is that winning an election for the Opposition in a one-party dominant state, where the PAP remains electorally dominant, represents a gargantuan challenge, both personally and professionally. For WP candidates, there can be no assumption of electoral success, particularly given the structural advantages enjoyed by the incumbent governing party.
No WP candidate can reasonably take for granted that he or she will win and become an MP, let alone approach the decision to stand for elections on the basis of achieving some degree of parity insofar as his or her renumeration prospects are concerned. We believe that our political system and our country is strengthened and not weakened by a strong and sensible Opposition in Parliament, where at least one third of the seats ought to be in Opposition hands.
[+7 sentences] A good Opposition plays a critical check and balance role and represents an important ballast in our political system. In March this year, the Government expressly confirmed that the 2026 Committee would not review the allowances of Legislative Assistants and Secretarial Assistants because this fell outside of the Committee's terms of reference.

Quality of Life and National Bonus

The speaker asks whether a broader social progress framework with objective and subjective measures will be considered, and notes the National Bonus recognises economy, jobs and incomes.

covers 10 highlighted sentences in 5 sections · also: Essential Household Expenditure Basket, NCSS Quality of Life data, National Bonus indicators
[+6 sentences]Mr Speaker, I agree that we should continue to attract capable and committed Singaporeans from different backgrounds to public service. Remuneration should never be the principal motivation for entering political office. But neither should we create unnecessary barriers that make it difficult for capable Singaporeans, particularly those with families and financial commitments, to step forward to serve. I would like to focus my comments on one of the recommendations, which is the proposal to explore the inclusion of a robust Quality of Life measure in the National Bonus framework. And as I speak, I declare my interest as a former Board Member of the National Council of Social Service (NCSS). I welcome this proposal.
Today, the National Bonus is determined by four economic and labour-market indicators: citizen unemployment, real income growth at the median, real income growth at the 20th percentile and real GDP growth.
[+5 sentences] These are important measures. Together, they ask whether our economy is growing, whether Singaporeans have jobs and whether incomes are rising, including for those at the lower end of the income distribution. The proposal to introduce Quality of Life presents us with an opportunity to ask a broader question: how should we measure whether Singaporeans are doing well? Sir, I believe that a Quality of Life measure should be part of the answer. And we do not have to start from scratch.
The NCSS has been measuring Quality of Life in Singapore for some years, using internationally established instruments, and so, we now have national reference data.
[+12 sentences] Could we use this opportunity to consider a broader framework of social progress? There are international precedents. New Zealand's Treasury, for example, uses a Living Standards Framework that considers multiple domains of individual and collective well-being. I am not suggesting that we import New Zealand's framework. Singapore has our own circumstances, priorities and social compact. But there is value in the underlying idea: economic performance and social progress are related, but they are not the same thing. I would offer four dimensions of social progress for consideration. First, material adequacy: do Singaporeans have enough to meet their essential needs? The National Bonus already monitors real income growth at the 20th percentile. This tells us whether lower-income Singaporeans are making economic progress. But growth and adequacy answer different questions. A household's real income can rise and yet remain insufficient to meet its essential needs.
Could we therefore consider developing an Essential Household Expenditure Basket?
[+18 sentences] Our Household Expenditure Survey published by the Department of Statistics already provides rich data about what households spend on housing, food, transport, healthcare, education and other needs. I am not proposing now what should go into the basket. Rather, could we establish a periodically updated measure of the resources required to meet a carefully defined set of essential household needs? We could then ask not only whether lower-income Singaporeans' incomes are rising, but whether fewer households lack the resources necessary for a basic but adequate standard of living. Second, access: can Singaporeans obtain essential services when they need them? One distinctive feature of Singapore's social compact is that wellbeing is not determined by household income alone. Singaporeans benefit from substantial public investment and support in areas such as housing, healthcare, education and social services. Social progress could therefore consider timely and effective access to essential services that I mentioned earlier, such as healthcare, public housing and preschool places, as well as early intervention and disability services. The precise measures require careful consideration. But the principle is important. For a parent waiting for early intervention for a child, a patient waiting for a necessary operation, or a family waiting for suitable housing, a service being available technically is different from being able to access it when needed. Third, social connectedness: do Singaporeans feel that they belong? A successful society is more than a collection of economically successful individuals. We are members of families, neighbourhoods, communities and a nation. We could therefore consider people's sense of belonging, the strength of their social support networks, or whether they feel connected to their communities. This matters because material living standards can rise even as people become more isolated from one another. Our economic indicators would not tell us if this were happening. Fourth, subjective wellbeing: do Singaporeans themselves feel that their lives are going well?
This brings me back to the Committee's proposal. I support the inclusion of a robust Quality of Life measure, but not all indicators need to be objective.
[+1 sentence] Objective indicators tell us about the circumstances in which people live.
A subjective measure allows Singaporeans themselves to tell us how they experience their lives.
[+1 sentence] Sir, I am not proposing today that these four dimensions be directly added to the National Bonus formula.
I am suggesting that as the Government develops its Quality of Life measure, we take the opportunity to develop a broader framework for understanding social progress.
[+11 sentences] There are technical questions to resolve. And any measure used must be robust, consistent over time and resistant to gaming. We should also be careful about holding the Government accountable for outcomes over which they have limited influence. But these challenges should not prevent us from asking the larger question. Our existing National Bonus indicators provide a strong picture of economic progress. The Committee's Quality of Life recommendation gives us an opportunity to complement this with a clearer conception of social progress. Mr Speaker, in conclusion, economic indicators tell us whether Singapore is prospering. Social indicators can tell us whether Singaporeans are flourishing. I have suggested four questions for consideration: do Singaporeans have enough to meet their essential needs? Can they access essential services when they need them? Do they feel that they belong?
And do Singaporeans themselves judge their quality of life to be good? So, as Government considers and develops the proposed Quality of Life measure, will it consider a broader social progress framework incorporating objective as well as subjective measures? If we can do this well, the National Bonus will continue to recognise the importance of a strong economy, jobs and rising incomes, whilst also recognising the reason these ultimately matter: to enable Singaporeans, their families and our communities to flourish.

[+1 sentence]Mr Speaker, in Mandarin.
(In Mandarin): Mr Speaker, in 2007, about a year after I entered Parliament, the Government moved a Motion to adjust the salaries of political appointment holders.
[+25 sentences] At the time, I did not take part in that debate. At that time, I was not entirely convinced that ministerial salaries should be pegged to the market. Although I understood the reasoning behind it, one question remained in my mind: was this the best approach? Twenty years have passed. I am older now, with more life and work experience and I hope, a little more wisdom. I know this remains an emotive issue, but I believe it is still necessary to share my views. Mr Speaker, besides having the privilege of serving as a Member of Parliament, I have also worked in the financial sector for more than 30 years. My years of political service and corporate work have given me the opportunity to understand, from two different perspectives, the distinction between national leadership and corporate leadership. As Members of Parliament, our responsibilities include holding the Government to account and reviewing policies. We also have the opportunity to work closely with Ministers and observe how they analyse issues, formulate policies, manage crises and make major decisions. In my professional work in finance, I have also worked extensively with corporate management teams, giving me a deep understanding of the business acumen and judgement required of corporate leaders, as well as the responsibilities and pressures they bear. My experience across these two fields has made me deeply aware that the duties and responsibilities borne by political and corporate leaders are fundamentally different in both nature and scale. A corporate leader must run the company well, manage profits and costs, and be accountable to customers, employees and shareholders. A political leader, however, bears responsibility for the entire country. This encompasses economic development, national security, people’s livelihoods, social cohesion and more – ultimately ensuring that Singaporeans' lives and livelihoods are protected today and in the future. We all know that Singapore has many inherent constraints. We are a tiny nation with no natural resources and a limited domestic market. Therefore, governing Singapore well is a formidable task. The Prime Minister and Ministers must constantly confront structural constraints and external shocks, assess developments accurately, weigh the national interest, and make decisive and sound decisions at critical moments. This is why our nation-building journey has never been smooth and why we have faced severe crises from time to time. How the Government’s leaders respond to crises is one of the most direct tests of leadership. Over the past few decades, whether during the 2008–2009 Global Financial Crisis or, more recently, the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, I witnessed how the Government’s leadership team responded in a steady, decisive and pragmatic manner, working at every turn to cushion the impact on Singaporeans’ lives and the economy. The international environment and the rapid pace of technological change will become even more complex. The Government's leadership team will undoubtedly face many tests again. Beyond the Government's effective crisis management, I have also seen, over the years, its foresight and ability to execute long-term plans while preparing for adversity in times of stability.
More than 20 years ago, before energy security became a major issue, we had already begun planning and building a liquefied natural gas terminal, giving Singapore more diversified sources of natural gas. Before biomedicine became a major industry, the Government had already committed substantial resources to building Biopolis and nurturing a research, talent and industry ecosystem.
[+1 sentence] Today, Singapore has built an internationally competitive ecosystem in biomedicine and scientific research.
To strengthen Singapore's position as an international financial centre and business hub, we began planning and developing Marina Bay decades ago, laying the foundations for the vibrant global city we see today. Before water security became a widely recognised global concern, Singapore had already begun developing NEWater.
[+30 sentences] At the same time, we have pursued long-term urban planning and preserved important green spaces and nature reserves. Behind these decisions lies a steadfast conviction: that this Little Red Dot must continue to survive, continue to develop, and continue to shine on the world stage. This requires Government leaders who are prepared to look further ahead, invest resources today, shoulder responsibility and act with the long term in mind. By the same token, the substantial national reserves we have today did not materialise out of thin air. They are the result of successive Governments maintaining fiscal discipline and prudent financial management over the long term, building them up bit by bit. Today, managing and safeguarding this vast national asset is an exceptionally weighty responsibility. This requires not only sound institutions and system, but also capable Ministers with good judgement and a deep understanding of the economy, finance and markets to provide stewardship and oversight, and to make the right decisions in the country's long-term interests. These many experiences have strengthened my conviction that: Singapore needs a political leadership team of the highest calibre and capability. This is one of our key advantages. However, high-quality and capable political leadership can never be taken for granted. How do we ensure that the best people are willing to enter public service and shoulder the responsibility of leading the country? First, they must of course possess a spirit of service, as well as integrity, honesty and the right values. A spirit of service and integrity are non-negotiable prerequisites. I believe no one would disagree with this. The next consideration is talent and ability. Ministers bear the weighty responsibility of governing the country and safeguarding the people. We need leaders with ability, resolve and perseverance. But we also know that outstanding people often have a corresponding market value. They are sought not only by the Government, but also by companies and other organisations eager to recruit and retain them. Therefore, if the salaries of political appointment holders remain disconnected from the market over the long term and the gap continues to widen, I fear that it will become increasingly difficult for future Governments to attract outstanding people into politics to lead the country. Mr Speaker, I believe most people would agree that, in the workplace, a person’s ability, experience and judgement, as well as the responsibilities he bears, should command a reasonable market value. We must then ask if that person chooses to enter politics, does his or her existing market value suddenly disappear? Should his and her abilities, experience and professional value, as well as the opportunities he gives up, be disregarded entirely? This is a question that deserves serious pondering. Of course, I fully agree that entering politics is, first and foremost, a public service. Holding public office also entails a degree of personal sacrifice. I have no disagreement with that. However, I believe that a spirit of service and reasonable remuneration are not mutually contradictory concepts. The two can certainly coexist. In my view, the existing ministerial salary framework is the balance that we are seeking.
The current framework uses market pay as a reference point and applies a 40% discount to reflect the dedication and sacrifice inherent in public service. In this round of adjustments, the Prime Minister has gone further by moderating the increase, such that serving Ministers will initially receive only a one-off salary adjustment capped at 9%.
[+19 sentences] Mr Speaker, over the years, Singapore has been fortunate to have successive generations of outstanding and capable leaders who have taken the country forward. Through working with the Prime Minister and Ministers, I have come to appreciate deeply that they are willing to take on this responsibility because of their sense of mission and dedication to Singapore. Let me cite Minister Vivian as an example. I have worked with Minister Vivian for more than 20 years. He is the anchor Minister for Holland–Bukit Timah GRC and Bukit Panjang Single Member Constituency (SMC). Since becoming Minister for Foreign Affairs in 2015, I have seen him represent Singapore with distinction on the international stage. He possesses keen strategic insight, thinks clearly, communicates forcefully, and consistently demonstrates a clear understanding of Singapore's strategic interests. As Minister for Foreign Affairs, he also keeps an extremely demanding schedule, travelling around the world throughout the year to protect Singapore's interests, expand our international space and strengthen partnerships. A few weeks ago, I asked Minister Vivian how he coped with such a packed and gruelling travel schedule year after year. He smiled and told me that, on some mornings, the first thing he had to ask himself upon waking in a hotel was: Which country am I in? What time zone is this? What engagements and agenda do I have today? This also shows that ministerial responsibilities demand not only intellectual capacity, but also energy and stamina. Let me give another example. During his 20 years as Prime Minister, Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong led Singapore through several major crises, while driving economic transformation, strengthening social protection and further consolidating Singapore's position as an international financial and business centre. In my interactions with Senior Minister Lee, I have keenly felt his profound sense of mission and responsibility towards Singapore. Let us also consider Prime Minister Lawrence Wong's journey in politics. More than a decade ago, before Prime Minister Wong entered politics, when he was the Chief Executive of the Energy Market Authority, I had the opportunity to meet him in my capacity as a banker. Even then, he left a deep impression on me.
He had not only a deep understanding of how the energy market operated, but also a firm grasp of the technical issues underlying power generation and energy systems. He later played a direct role in bringing Singapore's liquefied natural gas terminal project to fruition, giving us multiple sources of natural gas and further strengthening our energy security. Since taking office in 2024, Prime Minister Wong has led Singapore with calmness and steadiness through an increasingly turbulent global environment.
[+5 sentences] At the same time, he has refreshed our economic strategies, strengthened pro-family policies and continued to enhance social protection, laying the foundations for Singapore’s competitiveness and resilience in the next phase. He has said that when he was invited to enter politics, his original intention was simply to serve diligently and give back to the country; he never imagined that he would one day become Prime Minister. These examples reinforce my belief that those who genuinely choose to enter politics must first possess a sense of mission to serve the country. At the same time, we should not therefore assume that the personal opportunity costs they bear do not exist.
If we compare the salaries of the Prime Minister and Ministers with those of corporate executives, and then consider the responsibilities and pressures borne by each, I believe many would agree that: the sacrifices made by political appointment holders in fact far exceed the 40% discount reflected in the current salary framework.
[+2 sentences] Mr Speaker, as a small country, our margin for error in national governance is far smaller than that of many larger countries. We must therefore do all we can to avoid taking a meaningless pathway or paying needless costs.
Particularly in major national strategies and public policies, an error of judgement or a wrong turn could carry an enormous cost and might even set the country on a path of non-return. For this very reason, when selecting and bringing in national leaders, we cannot compromise on the quality of leadership.
[+1 sentence] Mr Speaker, ministerial salaries have remained unchanged for 15 years.
I agree that it is time for an adjustment.
[+2 sentences] I understand that many people still face a psychological hurdle in accepting that the salaries of political appointment holders should be linked to the market. Twenty years ago, I faced the same hurdle.
Twenty years on, I believe this is the right decision. If we want Singapore to continue to have an outstanding political leadership team in the decades ahead, we must establish a reasonable and sustainable system that encourages capable people of integrity and a strong sense of mission to step forward and serve the country.
[+1 sentence] I support the Ministerial Statement.

Leadership past and present

The passage credits Mr Lee Kuan Yew's team, Mr Goh Chok Tong, Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong and Prime Minister Lawrence Wong with Singapore's development and leadership.

covers 13 highlighted sentences in 6 sections · also: Comparable nations' leader remuneration, Fixed and variable salary split, Ministerial pay and public service
[+8 sentences]Mr Speaker, Sir, I rise today to address this House on a matter that touches the very heart of our social compact – the remuneration of our political office holders. I acknowledge that the Prime Minister has rightly framed that this is an emotive issue and indeed, it is. Let me begin by affirming what we all agree upon. I do not stand here to suggest that our leaders should toil for paltry sums. I fully accept the Government's three foundational pillars: first, that competitive pay is essential to prevent a debilitating talent drain to the private sector; second, that the "clean wage" principle, with its full transparency and absence of hidden perks, is a gold standard of integrity that we must defend; and third, that a performance-linked component ensures our Ministers remain relentlessly focused on the economic vitality of our nation. These are not trivial points. They are the architecture of a professional, corruption-free governance system that has served us well. However, Mr Speaker, the question before this House is not whether we should pay our office holders well.
The question is: what is the appropriate, defensible and principled basis for determining "how much is enough"?
[+1 sentence] Let me begin with the benchmark itself.
I wish to scrutinize the MR4 benchmark, which ties Ministerial salaries to the median income of the top 1,000 Singaporean earners, with a 40% discount.
[+8 sentences] So, I ask this House: why do we anchor national leadership compensation to the very apex of the private sector? The private sector exists to maximize shareholder value. It is a realm where cost-cutting, including the difficult decision to retrench workers, is often a necessary strategy for survival. But the Government, Mr Speaker, is not a corporation. The Government's mandate is fundamentally different from that of a private equity firm. Our leaders have a duty to protect jobs, not to eliminate them; to strengthen the social fabric, not merely to rationalize it; and to think in decades, not in quarterly earnings. If we are to look for comparators, should we not look across the globe to successful, stable democracies? The data is instructive.
The heads of government in Switzerland, Luxembourg, Denmark, Germany and Belgium – nations with comparable standards of living and governance standards – receive remuneration that is, at most, four to seven times their nation's median worker salary.
[+9 sentences] Mr Speaker, international news agencies have reported that Singapore already stands apart at the top of this list, paying our political leaders more than any other country. We are told that this adjustment is necessary to account for the opportunity costs of attracting top CEOs who earn between $6 million and $7 million. We must be clear. Public service is a calling, not a market transaction. The skillsets required to shepherd a nation through existential threats – pandemics, geopolitical fragmentation and climate change – are fundamentally distinct from those required to maximise a company's bottom line. One manages capital, the other manages the hopes and aspirations of millions of citizens. To equate the two is to misunderstand the moral weight of public office. We are also told that salaries have been frozen for 15 years and that an adjustment is simply overdue. But Mr Speaker, a delay in a review does not automatically justify a massive, uncompromising catch-up adjustment.
A more gradual and modest path, particularly given the 9% phased increase is already in motion, would have demonstrated fiscal prudence and social sensitivity.
[+6 sentences] Because, Mr Speaker, we must look at the ground we walk on. Today, we are witnessing the profound and disruptive rise of AI. Singaporeans are deeply anxious about housing costs, the trajectory of healthcare inflation, retirement adequacy and the relentless creep of the cost of living. In this climate, the Government must be exquisitely sensitive to the widening distance between the lived reality of the ordinary Singaporean and the remuneration of those who govern them. Perception matters as much as policy. That is why I now turn to my constructive proposal.
If we accept the premise of a clean wage, we must also accept the premise of shared risk. I propose that we adjust the structure to a fixed salary of 45% and a variable component of 55%.
[+2 sentences] Why this ratio? Because the fixed 45% already represents a substantial, dignified and generous sum that no office holder would struggle to live on.
The remaining 55% should be explicitly, transparently and heavily weighted toward national performance metrics that directly affect the median citizen – real median income growth, unemployment rates and housing affordability.
[+21 sentences] Under such a model, if the nation thrives, our leaders thrive with it, justly so. But if the nation faces headwinds, our leaders share in the national sacrifice. That is solidarity. And it ensures that the variable component is not a mere bonus, but a genuine reflection of the social contract between the governed and those who govern. Let me speak in Malay in my next speech. (In Malay): Mr Speaker, allow me to share a brief reflection from my travels. In the course of my work, I had the chance to witness many forms of governance across many nations. I have seen countries led by extraordinarily able individuals who lifted their people from despair into prosperity. I have also seen nations where poor leadership – driven by entitlement, corruption, or incompetence – squandered generational wealth and eventually left their people in dire situations. I have witnessed a country collapse into chaos, rise again with a change of government and then slide backward once more when complacency set in. The lesson, Mr Speaker, is this: good governance is critical. Singapore has been profoundly blessed because we have been led by great men and guided by leaders who are visionaries. (In English): Mr Speaker, allow me to share a brief reflection from my travels. In the course of my work, I have had the privilege of witnessing governance across many nations. I have seen countries led by extraordinarily able individuals who lifted their people from despair into prosperity. I have also seen nations where poor leadership, driven by entitlement, corruption or incompetence, squandered generational wealth and left entire populations destitute. I have witnessed a country collapse into chaos, rise again with a change of government and then slide backward once more when complacency sets in. The lesson, Mr Speaker, is this: good governance is critical. We have been profoundly blessed in Singapore. We have been managed by giants and navigated by visionaries. Singapore has been fortunate to have been served by Prime Ministers who led with conviction, empathy and resilience.
The late Mr Lee Kuan Yew, together with his pioneering team, transformed Singapore from a developing nation into a first world country within a single generation. [+19 sentences]Mr Speaker, political salaries will inevitably stir strong reaction. It is never entirely comfortable for any Parliament to debate how political office holders should be paid. Singapore has chosen a clean wage approach. Political remuneration is published. There are no hidden perks, and the framework is independently reviewed and debated in this house. We may disagree about the benchmark, the discount or how performance should be rewarded, but that transparency is itself a strength we should not take for granted. I also acknowledge the Prime Minister's decision to donate the full increase in his salary for the next five years or during his term. That is a personal decision, but the gesture should be recognised and it sends a clear message about his intentions that the salary increases are not about personal financial gain, but about ensuring that Singapore can continue to draw from and recognise capable people willing to serve. But today, we are discussing a compensation system with implications well beyond any one individual's intentions and potentially beyond a single term. So, my questions are not simply whether political office holders are paid too much or too little, they are whether we are valuing the right skills, rewarding the right outcomes and enabling capable people with the motivation to serve to step forward. I have three areas for the Government to consider. First, are we using the right reference group to benchmark Ministerial compensation? I accept the principle that Ministers should be compensated adequately. We should not design a system in which only those who are independently wealthy or willing to make very large financial sacrifices can afford to serve. The question is therefore how we determine what fair compensation should look like. There are two questions here that should be this that should be kept distinct. The first is what constitutes fair compensation for the role of a Minister and the second is a recruitment question – how broad a pool of potential candidates should compensation seek to keep open? What someone could earn elsewhere is relevant to the recruitment question, but it does not by itself tell us what the role of a Minister is fairly worth. These questions are related, but they are not the same today.
The MR4 benchmark is based on the median income of the top 1,000 Singapore Citizen earners, before applying the 40% discount for political service. The occupational breakdown is quite concentrated: 54.1% are in senior management positions; another 35.3% are in financial services; and the remaining 10.6% are professionals, such as lawyers, accountants, doctors and engineers.
[+13 sentences] How comparable are these roles to that of a Minister? A corporate executive may run a large and complex organisation, but the mandate is still bounded by organisational performance with economic outcomes as a central priority. For a Minister, economic performance is also critically important, but it is only one part of the mandate. A Minister must reconcile economic performance with distributional consequences, social cohesion, land constraints, national security resilience and inter-generational trade-offs. A financial trader may also earn very large sums by taking a leveraged position or exploiting arbitrage opportunities. That may require exceptional judgement, but it is very different from leading institutions, designing national policy and reconciling competing interests over long horizons. The fact that the role is highly paid does not by itself make it comparable to that of a Minister. My point, Sir, is not that people from these professions should not be recruited into political office. Some may make excellent political leaders. My question is why income should determine membership in the comparative group in the first place. The primary benchmark starts with those who earn the most and uses their earnings as its reference point. I suggest testing a different approach. Start with roles that reflect the skills, judgement, complexity and weight of responsibility we expect of political office holders, and that includes responsibility for decisions affecting Singaporeans, both today and far into the future.
Then, examine what people in those roles actually earn. I am not suggesting we abandon the current approach, but perhaps future reviews should test the top 1,000 benchmark against a role-based comparator constructed on this basis.
[+7 sentences] Whichever comparator group we use, there is a related question: how representative is a single year's income of what those individuals typically earn over time? If somebody earns $3 million today, do they typically command that income for three years, five years or 10 years? Or do earnings fluctuate because of bonus cycles, equity, realisation, business profits, or particularly good years? Persistence may also differ across occupations. Some partnerships in professional services have retirement or tenure limits. Professionals whose earnings depend heavily on personal practice, such as surgeons, may also face a finite period of peak earning capacity. So, annual realised income is not necessarily representative of long-term compensation.
And because Ministerial service typically unfolds over several years, we should also ask whether a one-year snapshot gives a representative picture of what people in that comparative group earn over a similar period. That is why I suggest examining three- or five-year average earnings, rather than relying only on a single year's realised income.
[+2 sentences] If the same people consistently command similar incomes over several years, then a one-year snapshot may be reasonable. But if there is substantial turnover of volatility, it tells us what someone earned in that year is not necessarily what people in comparable roles typically earn over a longer period.
On the second question, Sir, how wide the talent pool we should keep open.
[+8 sentences] Minister Chan has said that pay should ensure capable people are not deterred, but also that financial reward should not be their primary attraction. I agree wholeheartedly. The public may understandably worry that high salaries will attract people for the wrong reasons, or that financial incentives may crowd out the motivation to serve, but research on motivation and meaningful work suggest that the relationship is not so simple. If we want Singaporeans to have good choices at the ballot box, we should also ensure that capable Singaporeans have a realistic choice to put themselves forward. Mr Speaker, my suggestions are therefore not principally about finding a higher or lower number. They are about improving the architecture of the system.
First, identify roles that fairly reflect the skills, judgement and the weight of responsibility expected of our political office holders, and test the top 1000 benchmark against a role-based comparator. Second, examine the trajectory and persistence of earnings rather than relying only on a one-year snapshot when establishing the compensation benchmark. Third, once we have a credible comparator, replace the application of a political service discount with an adjustment that reflects the distinctive burden of political office.
[+2 sentences] In my view, those burdens support a compensating premium. Fourth, complement measures of current national performance with longer horizon over with a longer horizon view of stewardship.
Fifth, develop a standalone role-based framework for MP remuneration. And sixth, review whether the MP role itself is sustainable so that those who step forward can continue giving their best to Singaporeans over the long term.
[+2 sentences] Ultimately, the question is not simply about how much we pay. It is whether the system fairly recognises the skills required, the weight of responsibility and the distinctive burdens of political leadership, whether it rewards stewardship of both the present and the future, and whether it keeps the door open to capable Singaporeans who have both the ability and the motivation to serve.
