[+1 sentence]Mr Speaker, allow me to begin with some personal reflections.
For more than three decades before entering politics, I was in the private sector, practising first as a doctor. I later became involved in the business of healthcare as an entrepreneur, a founder of a healthcare enterprise, and subsequently as the head of a global private healthcare conglomerate Medicine has a way of teaching you what truly matters.
[+23 sentences] When I was a young student, my mother fell seriously ill, and this was the reason why I changed the course of my life and chose to study medicine instead. Medicine taught me a profound lesson. We always see, assess, we address the person holistically, before you diagnose, before you assess his problem. Before you even think about a diagnosis, you make efforts to listen and to comfort. Before you prescribe, you understand. In those days in the 1980s, we were taught as students that we cure seldom, we relieve often, but we must always, always comfort our patients. Over the years, my responsibilities grew beyond the consult room. I was privileged to lead healthcare organisations and businesses, with the opportunity to shape not just individual patient care, but healthcare systems that served hundreds of thousands of people. It was deeply meaningful and fulfilling work. It challenged me intellectually. It stretched me as a leader and yes, it also rewarded me handsomely. Yet, with each new responsibility came the same enduring lesson. My career decisions are my own but they have far-ranging effects on the people that I care about. To begin with, my family, my loved ones, my patients as well as employees, my business partners, stakeholders and investors – and the list goes on. My career trajectory was exciting. I was able to build, consolidate, reinforce a global platform to deliver more accessible and specialised care to patients around the world. I also had opportunities to do important deals, successfully acquire, integrate companies and put Singapore's healthcare industry onto the world map. For someone who came from humble beginnings, I did not have an easy time filling these multiple roles. There were multiple twists and turns, and inevitable hard knocks. At times, the road ahead seemed daunting and the burdens I carried too heavy. But I was fortunate, blessed to meet many people along the way. Many of them became good friends, partners, mentors, supporters; all helpers in my travails. People often ask me why I left all this behind.
The truth is there was not a single defining moment that led me to leave my fulfilling career for the hurly-burly of politics. It was a gradual but a growing inner realisation that whatever experience I had accumulated over those years in the private sector could perhaps be put to good use in a different way, not just to change a few lives at a time or to build an organisation, but to give back to my country and my people.
[+31 sentences] And so, when the opportunity came to serve, I stepped forward. I have often wondered how things would have been like if I had the opportunity to serve earlier, come in into politics in my 40s and not in my 50s. I have never regretted my years as a practising family physician nor have I regretted as a healthcare entrepreneur, for those years when you struggled through, shaped me into who I am today. But throughout my three decades in the private sector, I have also always viewed public service as a special calling; a special but tough calling. And true enough, that is what I found out when I came into the Government in 2020. The Government is unlike any organisation I have ever worked in. Every issue has multiple, many facets. No problem you encounter is a simple one. Each and every decision you make involves intense deliberation and consideration. And often you find yourself choosing between difficult trade-offs because each policy potentially affects millions of lives and far into the future. For me, the learning curve was not just steep; it was humbling. And Members of the House, it still is today. Even after decades of experience in leadership, I find myself having to learn something new every single day – learning how the Government really works, how policies intersect, learning to listen better, balancing competing interests and learning that good intentions alone are never enough. In fact, I still ask myself sometimes: did I make the right choice coming into politics? Have I given up too much? Am I really doing good to justify my choice of public service? The reality is that political service demands significantly more from those who choose to serve. The hours are longer. The responsibilities are heavier. Every decision is scrutinised, and there is little separation between public duty and private life. Running a Ministry is not a matter of chance or ruling of the dice, like "tikam tikam". You cannot make spur of the moment decisions: "Anyhow also can". It takes time, measured, calibrated deliberation to make the right policy calls. It takes careful consideration. There are times I wish I could have been better equipped for public office. Perhaps, if I had a longer runway, I could, in time, have contributed more, been more useful to Singapore. But Members of the House, therein lies the conundrum. For young professional executives, it is not easy to step away from careers that they have spent years, sometimes decades, building. Careers providing for loved ones, pursuing new opportunities, negotiating ambitious deals, climbing the corporate ladder. Give up all this and make a hard pivot into full-time public service just before you reach your peak in the private sector. This reflection brings me to the issue before us today.
Speaking only for myself, no realistic level of Ministerial salary could have matched what I was earning before I joined the Government.
[+9 sentences] And I could have gone on earning, chasing, making exciting new deals, setting up new enterprises for many more years had I stayed in the private sector. The reality is, had money been my primary consideration, I would have never entered politics. But I just felt I had to give back to the country and the people who had given me so much. I know that my own circumstances are unique. I cannot speak for everyone who is faced with the dilemma of either continuing to pursue their own careers or stepping into the uncertainties of public office. In my case, by the time I entered politics, I had already spent decades building many companies in the private sector. Ministerial clean wage compensation

Singapore compensates Ministers transparently through a clean wage, with no hidden allowances, so they are not incentivised to look elsewhere.

covers 17 highlighted sentences in 8 sections · also: Allowances and demands on office holders, Courage, conviction, principle over expediency, MP remuneration inflation increase
[+20 sentences]Sir, every political system must answer one unavoidable question. How should those entrusted with the highest offices of government be remunerated? Every political system has to compensate its political office holders. Do we look at other countries? Sometimes, yes; sometimes, no; often, no. Take the United Kingdom (UK), for example, once a byword for rectitude and probity among its public servants. Ministerial salaries there have been frozen for years, causing them to fall significantly in real terms over time. Britain has repeatedly found itself in difficult situations. Former Prime Minister Boris Johnson became embroiled in controversy over a Conservative Party donor financing the refurbishment of his Downing Street flat. Unfortunately, the questions do not end when politicians leave office. In other words and in other countries, many senior public officials routinely move between government and major corporations, investment banks, lobbying organisations and other private firms. To them, public office is often merely one chapter in a much longer professional career. For example, former UK's Prime Minister Tony Blair went on to build an extensive portfolio of advisory appointments, consultancy work and speaking engagements after leaving 10 Downing Street. This phenomenon is not unique to the UK. In the United States, the Americans called it the revolving door. Even former Presidents have earned substantial sums through books, speaking engagements and corporate deals after leaving office. Again, there is nothing inherently unlawful about any of thisthis, but ‒ and here is the nub ‒ it illustrates a very different model of politics from ours. Financial rewards may not come during public office, they come afterwards in some other countries. Such a system creates different incentives. If politicians know that their future careers may depend on relationships built while in office, the public will inevitably wonder whether today's decisions are made solely in the national interest or whether tomorrow's opportunities are also at the back of the minds of their leaders. From the beginning with the founding Prime Minister, Singapore deliberately chose a different path.
Rather than expecting Ministers to rely on gifts, outside interest or other lucrative opportunities after leaving office, Singapore compensates them transparently through a clean wage, one that is sufficient to ensure that they are not incentivised to look elsewhere to make up the difference. It means every Singaporean knows exactly how Ministers are remunerated. There are also no hidden allowances, no need to spend one's time in office preparing for the next career.
[+5 sentences] You try to cultivate outside interest for personal gain before you leave office, you could well be invited to the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau. Our system preserves the independence of our Ministers as good government requires. Political courage to push for the right thing, to see it through for the long term has been critical to Singapore's success. Finding good people is paramount but keeping them in means setting up political careers for longevity. We ask our Ministers to make difficult decisions that may not always be popular – building reserves instead of spending them, restructuring industries before crises emerge, investing for future generations, making choices whose benefits may only become apparent years later.
They must be able to do so without worrying about planning or pleasing benefactors, cultivating future employers or positioning themselves for life after politics. This is what our model of Ministerial salaries seeks to guarantee: that Ministers owe their loyalty, judgement and decisions to one group only ‒ Singaporeans.

[+27 sentences]Mr Speaker, it has been 15 years since the salary of political appointment holders and MPs were last revised. In the meantime, prices and wages in Singapore have risen considerably. A revision of salaries is therefore timely. However, the argument to raise salaries, particularly those of Ministers and political office holders, is not an easy or straightforward one to make. There are at least two reasons for this. First, because we want leaders who serve out of sense of duty and passion for the country rather than pecuniary considerations; and second, because political talent and capability cannot simply be measured by the market wage that one commands. The argument for higher pay must be framed sensitively in a way that the public can understand and accept. The Government must be particularly careful to avoid giving the impression that the only talent who are valued are those who command high salaries or that would be impossible to attract capable, competent people to political office without high wages. Otherwise, the argument for raising Ministerial wages will not land. Broadly speaking, potential recruits to political office could fall into one of three groups. The first are those for whom salary matters little. Among them are some who have already accumulated considerable wealth so that pay is no longer a key consideration for them. The second group may come from sectors and occupations that do not pay premium wages, or they may have yet to reach the senior, high-paying position within the organisations. For them, taking up political office may not entail a financial sacrifice and could in some cases mean an increase in income. But for the third group, compensation may be a deciding factor in whether they try for political office. These could be senior permanent secretaries in the public sector or successful professionals or executives in the private sector for whom any significant drop in pay could affect their financial commitments. While I do not know the size of the third group, appropriate compensation can help ensure that we do not unnecessarily narrow the pool of senior professionals from whom political leaders might be recruited. This matters to Singapore for the reasons the Prime Minister highlighted in his Ministerial Statement – that Singapore needs capable leadership and the best mix of talent to steer the country forward. I see a parallel between this issue and another that has been recently discussed, which is whether greater financial support for parenthood will be effective in raising Singapore's fertility rate, To address the birth rate, many Singaporeans have expressed the view that money alone cannot move the needle. For people to start and grow families, they must want children and see parenthood as meaningful. Yet for many couples, the cost of raising children is an issue and more generous financial support could, for some, tilt the balance in favour of starting a family or having another child. Likewise, pay cannot and should not be the principal motivation for someone to seek political office. Yet for some, the financial sacrifice, on top of other sacrifices, may be what tilts the balance one way or the other. We have to hold in our minds two concepts – the idealism of service and the pragmatism of pay. Both may be pertinent to someone weighing up an entry into politics. Let me now turn to the larger issue of how to expand the pool of talent for political office, which is so critical to Singapore's continued success. Just like the fertility challenge, there is a need to factor in both financial and broader considerations.
Many of us would like to see more leaders and senior professionals from the private sector step forward to serve. But for those new to political or public service, it would usually be appropriate for them to start in junior political appointments rather than lead a Ministry in the first instance. The salary scales of junior political office holders must therefore be sufficiently flexible to accommodate them. One possibility that could be considered as a transitional arrangement for those taking especially large pay cuts – for instance, giving them 60% of their last drawn pay, subject to an appropriate cap and limited to the first two or three years before their pay reverts to the normal benchmark for their substantive appointment.
[+1 sentence] Promising private sector candidates should be encouraged to step forward to contest elections and serve in political office without the assumption or expectation that all or even a majority must remain in office for the long haul.
Some may wish to serve for a limited period while others may find that political office is not a good fit after all. There should be no stigma attached to going back to the private sector after a term as an office holder.
[+3 sentences] Nor should we look only to the private sector. As my fellow Nominated Member of Parliament Mark Lee reminded me, our political leadership can be further strengthened by perspectives from the non-profit sector. I am glad that we have Parliamentary colleagues from this sector and I hope to see more people with non-profit backgrounds serve in political office in future.
The overall aim is to lower the barriers to entry for individuals while giving Singapore a wider pool of potential political talent, from which future Cabinet Ministers may be drawn.
[+2 sentences] The Government will also benefit from the diversity of ideas and experiences that those from the private and non-profit sectors bring during their time in office. It is certainly not my place to advise any political party on how it should go about its recruitment, but I hope that public discourse will go beyond the question of how much political office holders should be paid to the broader question of how Singapore can continue to attract people of ability, integrity and commitment from diverse backgrounds to step forward and serve.
Ultimately, the objective is not high pay in itself, but a wider and stronger pool of people willing and able to take on the responsibilities of political leadership.

Ministerial salary principles and differences

The parties agree on principles and moves this term, differing mainly on the formula and MR4 reference salary.

covers 40 highlighted sentences in 18 sections · also: Assessing Ministers, CDCs and Mayors value, Committee areas for study
[+28 sentences]Mr Speaker, I thank all Members who have spoken in this debate. I will respond to the broader issues that have been raised and Minister Chan will address the specific issues relating to the salary framework. I have listened to all the speeches earlier and I am glad there is considerable common ground across this House. This was also the case when the Parliament debated political salaries in 2012. Then, there was broad agreement that salaries should be competitive enough to enable us to recruit people of the necessary calibre while incorporating a substantial discount to reflect the ethos of service. We have heard essentially the same principles affirmed in this debate, by People Action's Party (PAP) MPs, by Mr Pritam Singh of the WP and also the Nominated MPs who spoke up. That common ground is important. It means that the central question before us is not whether political service should be competitively remunerated, or whether there should be a discount for public service. We agree on both. The differences are over how the framework should be calibrated and how the revised framework should be implemented. So, there are two distinct issues: first, what should be the structure for political salaries, which was the focus of the review Committee; and second, given the Committee's recommendations, how should the Government implement them. Let me first deal with the structure. Some Members asked whether the benchmark should continue. To refer to the top 1,000 Singaporean earners, and whether the resulting reference salary is too high. The review Committee did not simply take the existing formula as given. It examined the framework afresh. It considered whether the reference group remain relevant, whether it contain a sufficiently broad range of occupations and professions, and whether the resulting salary levels were fair and reasonable. And there is an important point here. The benchmark does not mean that we intend to recruit our political leaders only from these 1,000 individuals. Plainly, we do not. The benchmark is a reference point. It seeks to capture in a broad and objective way the opportunity cost faced by the sort of people we hope will step forward for political service: people with the ability and experience to take on very demanding national responsibilities whether they come from the private sector, the public service, the professions or elsewhere. After reviewing the evidence, the Committee concluded the basic formula remains sound while recommending several refinements. And this is not the conclusion of one committee alone. This is now the third time we have convened an independent review committee on political salaries. The first Committee in 2012 proposed the formula. The Committee in 2017 affirmed the formula. The present Committee has examined it again and reached the same broad conclusion.
Under the formula which has not changed, the MR4 reference salary rises from $1.1 million to $1.8 million. Seen on it on its own, that is a substantial increase, but we should also understand why the gap has opened up, because the benchmark has effectively remained unchanged for 15 years, while salaries elsewhere in the economy have continued to move.
[+8 sentences] And it is not just the private sector. Consider senior Permanent Secretaries and Appellate Judges. Their remuneration is determined under different frameworks for different roles, but their reference salaries are now higher than the MR4 benchmark. Not just the current MR4 benchmark but also the revised MR4 benchmark of $1.8 million. I am not suggesting that these other salaries should be lower. Quite the opposite. We need first rate people in the Civil Service and Judiciary, just as we need them in political leadership. Nor am I saying that ministerial salaries should just match theirs.
The point is that different remuneration frameworks constructed for different senior public responsibilities have arrived at broadly comparable orders of magnitude and the Ministerial benchmark continues to be lower than what we pay for other positions carrying the highest levels of public responsibilities, because political service incorporates a more substantial discount. There is a perception that civil servants joining politics enjoy a pay increase.
[+2 sentences] I want to dispel that myth. That does not happen.
There is no increase when civil servants join politics. Sometimes, it is even a pay cut, and when you look at the earnings over subsequent years for civil servants, if they had stayed on and done well, they would very likely have earned more in the Civil Service, as I have explained just now.
[+41 sentences] Some Members have noted that there are countries which pay their ministers less but nevertheless achieve good governance outcomes. So, they ask why should political salaries go up further? It is a fair question, but as several Members have also noted, international comparisons of political salaries have to be treated with care. First, headline salaries alone do not tell the full story. We have to look at each system in its entirety. In many countries, the overall remuneration of office holders extend beyond the official salary. There may be pensions allowances, housing, or other benefits, as well as arrangements that provide support after political office. These do not appear in the headline salary, so comparisons based simply on the published annual salary can be misleading. More importantly, different countries organise political leadership and government in very different ways, reflecting their own traditions and institutions. For example, in some countries, responsibilities are distributed across national, regional and local governments. In Singapore, we are a city state with a single national government, where a very wide range of responsibilities, economic, social security and municipal all come together at the centre. There are also differences in how political leadership is developed. In many countries, governments and ministers change more frequently. Some ministers may come in from the private sector, serve for a few years, and then return to their previous careers. Others spend much of their time and energy managing politics and the immediate electoral cycle. The ministers then rely more heavily on the civil service or teams of advisors to develop and carry the policy agenda. We see this when we exchange notes with our overseas counterparts. Singapore has developed a different model. Yes, our Ministers are politicians. They must contest elections and win the confidence of voters, but once elected and in office, they are expected to govern, to master their briefs, lead their Ministries, and do so with a longer-term perspective. So, they cannot just preside over the Ministry as a non-executive chairman. They have to set the tone and direction, make the big decisions. They direct the work of their teams, and that means empowering their officers, bringing out the best in them, helping to clear roadblocks and obstacles, and working together to get things done. And when major reforms are needed, our Ministers have to lead from the front. They develop the case for change, bring the public along, work through the implementation and see the reforms through. In Singapore, we expect our Ministers to be effective politicians, effective executives and effective leaders. That is how we have operated our system and that is how we have achieved exceptional results. I am not saying that our model is better or that others should follow us. Every country must develop arrangements that work in its own circumstances. The relevant question for us is not, can another country make a different model work? Clearly, some can. The relevant question is, what arrangements will enable Singapore to sustain high-quality political leadership over the long term. If we fail to attract enough good people into political leadership, there will be consequences. The problems will not appear overnight. Government does not stop functioning because good people choose not to enter politics. But the effects accumulate gradually, through successive rounds of recruitment and leadership renewal. Over 15, 20, 25 years, the difference will be visible – in the quality of political leadership, in the decisions the Government makes and eventually, in the quality and effectiveness of the Civil Service as well. By the time such deterioration becomes obvious, rebuilding the system will be much harder. Perhaps, even impossible. We do not claim that the present formula is perfect. That is why there will continue to be regular independent reviews.

MR4 benchmark not entitlement

The new MR4 benchmark is a reference point, not an entitlement, with capped adjustments and no near-term move to $1.8 million.

We also thank Member Mr Azhar Othman for his suggestions to vary the variable component in the salary package. We have heard two different perspectives. There is one perspective that calls for a higher variable component, perhaps a bit more like the private sector. There is also another perspective that calls for a smaller variable component or a higher fixed component, given the nature of the job.
The Committee has considered all this and on balance, they felt that the current two third, one third split is about right.
[+12 sentences] We will continue to look at this as we gain more experience running this framework. Member Dr Haresh Singaraju also suggested to have clearer targets published to ascertain the effectiveness of political leadership. We understand and we can share with him this sentiment. But as I have mentioned, governance is not just about a series of KPIs, and certainly not a series of KPIs for this year alone. So, we will have to be careful how and what we publish, but I think he has raised a very important point. There are many things that we may not be able to publish. How do we account for the tough negotiations that the Ministry of Trade and Industry has to undertake behind the scenes to secure our trade agreements? And hopefully, we never have to tell Singaporeans one day that the threat has emerged without us knowing. So, we will try and we will continue to keep our minds open on what are the KPIs that we can share and how to share with fellow Singaporeans in such a way that you will not distort our perspective of thinking long-term and managing issues, preempting issues before they catch fire. Sir, some Members may understandably also be concerned about the financial impact arising from the updates to the framework. As the Prime Minister has shared, the impact is expected to remain stable.
Assuming the maximum 9% adjustment, overall spending on political appointment holder salaries is expected to remain below 0.05% of government expenditure and below 0.01% of GDP.

[+4 sentences] It served as a broad proxy. If we go back a bit in history, to when this framework was first started, actually, we chose a certain number from certain vocations. But at the end of the day, regardless of which formula and which benchmark we choose, we still need to ask one basic question: will this benchmark, will this framework allow the Prime Minister, any Prime Minister, to have the range and the flexibility to bring in that three archetypes that I talked about?
[+27 sentences] The new entrant with potential, the experienced colleague to continue to stay, the established individual who is prepared to come in and join us, having had a successful career somewhere else. So, we will continue to study this. On the idea of doing, it on a multi-year basis, we have also considered that. It is a fair idea because as many have said, the performance of the Government cannot be measured year by year. Then, the question is, how many years and what to do if there is a change of government. So, those are practical difficulties as we consider these particular suggestions. I have been to different Ministries, from the Ministry of Social and Family Development to the Ministry of Trade and Industry, the Ministry of Education, and now the Ministry of Defence. And I would say that in all the Ministries the time cycle for results are all very different. When I was in the Ministry of Social and Family Development, someone asked me, how do you define success? Is it how much ComCare you have given out? How many people you have helped? I said no. In fact, the more ComCare we have to give, it is not a mark of success. The mark of success is how little we need to give out ComCare. But that is a shorter-term goal. The real mark of success for the Ministry of Social and Family Development is when we help somebody, will that child one day grow up feeling confident, independent and say, "I can take care of myself and my family". That is a generational thing. When I was in the Ministry of Education, what defines the success of the Ministry of Education? Surely, not the Primary School Leaving Exams (PSLE) scores or the GCE "A" Level scores. It is whether one generation later, our young people grow up and have the confidence, look at the world and say, "Whatever challenges there may be out there, I will be able to overcome them, either individually or with my Team Singapore". Success will be that even when the chips are down, our younger generation will say, "I will be here in spite of". These are long-term challenges that are hard to measure. In the Ministry of Defence, when I returned last year, some of the projects that I initiated and work on 20 years ago are now coming on stream. So, we are fully cognisant of the challenges of using a single year measure, but we are also cognisant of the challenges of using a multi-year assessment metrics. We will have to find that balance. Ultimately, as Member Ms Yeo Wan Ling has said deep inside each of us, every Singaporean will have to answer the question, "Has this team delivered? On the standalone framework for the MPs and the Mayors, we agree with the Committee's recommendation that we should examine the benchmark. The best chance for any Prime Minister to assemble a team that is worthy of Singapore. covers 6 highlighted sentences in 3 sections · also: Employer reimbursement for child-related leave, Enhanced child-related leave and support
As announced by the Prime Minister at the National Day Rally, the Government will enhance child-related leave, financial support, caregiving and housing measures to provide greater confidence and assurance to Singaporeans in starting and raising families.
[+4 sentences] These enhancements are the first set of recommendations from the Marriage and Parenthood Reset Workgroup.  Parents have asked when the Childcare Leave enhancements will take effect. This will take some time. Legislative amendments are required, and we are working with our tripartite partners on the implementation details.
We also need to give employers time to manage the operational impact of the Childcare Leave enhancements. We will share more details by early next year.
[+1 sentence]  We hear employers' concerns about the operational challenges of implementing the increased Childcare Leave, as well as the impact on the rest of the wider workforce.
As announced, the Government will reimburse employers for the full duration of all child-related leave, up to a cap.
[+6 sentences] Employers may use this increased reimbursement to support covering arrangements, including by hiring temporary staff or recognising employees who take on additional covering responsibilities. We are also studying ways to better support companies with backfilling arrangements. The longer-term solution to this issue is for workplaces to recognise and accept that leave for caregiving needs, such as parental leave, is now part and parcel of normal human resources (HR) policy and to plan and design their workplace norms and practices around this. This would include job redesign, flexible work arrangements, short-term covering arrangements and where appropriate, artificial intelligence (AI) and automation. All employees, not only parents with children, but also singles and married persons without children will benefit from improved workplace culture and norms that help them to better balance work and personal responsibilities, including caregiving needs. To this end, we are working with employers, tripartite partners and other stakeholders to foster work-life friendly practices and will study Ms Cassandra Lee’s suggestion for an accreditation mark to recognise work-life friendly workplaces.

[+17 sentences]I thank Mr Low for his supplementary questions. In a sense, both supplementary questions are linked because they have to do with how the employee is regarded in the workplace. [+5 sentences]I thank Ms Tan for her question. As I have shared earlier, the 80% personal income tax relief cap is intended to make our personal income tax system more progressive. And for mothers with more children, about seven in 10 individuals claiming the Working Mother's Child Relief on two or three children, are in fact, not affected by the cap. So, after studying the pattern of reliefs claimed, we decided to limit the total reliefs that one can claim to $80,000 from the year of assessment 2018, because the relief cap does not affect about 98% of tax resident individuals.

[+1 sentence]Mr Speaker, the United States Trade Representative (USTR) has concluded its Section 301 investigation into imports associated with forced labour and imposed a 12.5% tariff rate on imports from Singapore.  
About one-third of Singapore's domestic exports to the US, or around $9.5 billion, are exposed to this 12.5% tariff. This is about 3% of our total domestic exports globally. In addition to optical instruments and chemical products, the other products in Singapore that are affected by the 12.5% tariff include offshore drilling and production platforms, and precious metals. Furthermore, the additional 2.5% in tariff compared to the earlier 10% tariff imposed under Section 122 is equivalent to an estimated 0.7 percentage point increase in Singapore's overall effective tariff rate with the US.
[+1 sentence] We are assessing a range of economic indicators, including sectoral economic performance and labour market structure metrics, as well as firms’ outlook and expectations.

[+5 sentences]Sir, before I begin to answer the questions, I also like to share with the House that, coincidentally, today is World Suicide Prevention Day. I am sure all of us would like to take this opportunity to grieve with those who have lost loved ones, honour the courage of those who have held on and encourage those who are still struggling. To Ms He's questions, the data on suicide deaths is published by the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority annually, based on data from the Report on Registration of Births and Deaths. For youths, suicide can appear as a leading cause of death because deaths from illnesses are uncommon at these ages. And male suicide rates are also observed to be significantly higher across nearly all developed economies.
Overall, Singapore’s suicide rate is generally lower compared to other developed economies. We note the increase in suicides among those aged 30 to 39 in 2024, following a relatively stable trend in the preceding years.
[+5 sentences] Every suicide is painful. We must continue to prevent suicides as best as we can. However, suicide is multifactorial. Based on a study by the Institute of Mental Health (IMH) last year, suicide may be associated with ongoing physical health issues, breakdown in significant relationships or a combination of factors. Poor mental health is also a contributor of suicide.
Strengthening mental resilience and encouraging early help-seeking are therefore key to suicide prevention. These are being implemented through the National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy.
[+2 sentences]  Broader yet salient factors to prevent suicides are a stable society, peace and stability, supportive family environment, supported by a good education system, public housing and healthcare system. We will continue to monitor the effectiveness of our measures.

[+8 sentences]Sir, I thank the Member, Ms He, for her three supplementary questions. And I agree with her. Behind every suicide statistic is a person, and family and friends who care for them; and every suicide is something that we care deeply about. This morning, I was with the Samaritans of Singapore, speaking with the counsellors and volunteers at the frontline, speaking to people who have lost loved ones to suicides, and speaking to suicide survivors. And it is hard work. This is something that requires the collective effort of society, not just the Government, but also community organisations and for all of us to play an important role. And so, I thank the Member for raising this important issue. Let me address her third question first, which is a more technical question regarding the provisional numbers. 
The reason why we publish the figures in a timely manner, even though those might be provisional and would be updated later on, is to ensure there is transparency; that there is in enough information out there – for the purpose of transparency, for us to make decisions and to understand the trends and understand how we can better support those who are in need. The reason why there is a time lag between the provisional numbers and the ones that are to be updated later on is because the provisional number of deaths reported in the annual report on Registration of Births and Deaths are based on those confirmed to be suicides at the time of the publication of the report.
[+10 sentences] At the time of the publication, there could, in addition, be a number of unnatural death cases which are still pending an outcome from the coroner's inquiry. So, they are pending the coroner's inquiry. These cases are captured in the same report under the header "Symptoms, signs and abnormal clinical and laboratory findings not elsewhere classified". We are transparent in publishing all the figures but some of the figures in that category have not been confirmed as suicide by the coroner. Some of these cases may then subsequently be classified as suicides after the coroner's inquiry and the number of suicides for that year will be updated. So, it is a process that we go through and we are working very closely with the different agencies to ensure those numbers are updated in a timely manner. But really, we publish those figures on a regular basis for transparency reasons. So, that is the third supplementary question. For the other two supplementary questions. The first one on men, the Member is right to highlight men.
For many years, men have made up the majority of suicide deaths.
[+2 sentences] And we have seen similar patterns across the world internationally. One difficult reality is that sometimes the person who needs help may be the one least likely to ask for it.
But we cannot design a system that depends only on someone putting up their hand. So, we are taking a holistic approach: making sure to reduce stigma to improve suicide literacy, but also to help families, friends, colleagues and communities to recognise distress and connect someone to help.
[+23 sentences] There was a very nice, lovely Forum letter in Lianhe Zaobao today written by someone who has spent time volunteering in suicide prevention work. His message is, I think, a very timely one. He asked are we prepared to listen when we ask someone "How are you?". And oftentimes, the person may express distress, but are we really willing to listen? That applies to all of us – colleagues, friends, classmates. We are working together with community partners to make sure that those in distress know where help is. There is no point having services and help available, but they are not reachable. Which brings me to the reply to Ms He's second question. Whether there is a formal strategy, I think it is a separate matter. But practically, we are already implementing many of the programmes together with our community partners across different initiatives, focusing not just at the point of help. Someone in distress who has symptoms and has signs even before they pick up the hotline to call, or even before they show up in our hospitals or medical institutions. And how are we building the mental health and resilience in our population, especially young people from early age, whether through The Youth Resilience plan, building up resilience in our young people, strengthening protective factors over the longer term. Or post-crisis youths; those who are discharged from hospitals, because the crisis does not end there. How do you prevent them from having distress and social triggers again? When they are discharged from hospital or out of institutions, how do we work with community partners to better support them to get back to living? And how do we make sure that we mange crisis in a much more coordinated manner across different parties: healthcare, education institutions, community groups, volunteer groups. We are working on those and efforts are in place. And fourthly, suicide literacy. We are investing a lot more to raise literacy on suicide, not just people who are going through distress and thinking about help, but also family, friends and colleagues around them on how to show support and pick up changes in behaviour, changes in perhaps attitudes and perspectives on life. So, we are raising suicide literacy. Underlying all this is building up the research and data to support and inform our initiatives. These things are in progress. We are working hard on those initiatives with our community partners and more importantly, I think, it is a reminder that it is a whole-of-society, whole-of-community effort.

Humanitarian concerns and public order

Humanitarian concerns must not undermine public order, national security or stability, and foreigners must not use Singapore for political causes.

covers this turn's highlighted sentences · summary of Criteria to Distinguish Prohibited Political Advocacy from Expressions of Humanitarian Concern in Assessing Artists’ Conduct Relating to International Conflicts
[+2 sentences]Sir, the Government recognises the humanitarian impact of international conflicts and that artists may wish to express concern for those affected. Such expressions are not, in themselves, prohibited.  
While humanitarian concerns can be expressed in different ways, it should not undermine public order, national security or stability in Singapore. This condition is made clear in the Arts Entertainment Classification Code issued by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), which all licensees are required to comply with. Moreover, Singapore should not be used by foreigners as a platform to further political causes, including those relating to conflicts or political issues overseas.
[+1 sentence] Artists performing in Singapore, both locals and foreigners, are expected to comply with our laws and the conditions of their licence during their event.
Besides the intent of their actions, IMDA will consider the likely impact of their performance to assess if the conditions are met.

[+7 sentences]Sir, on rain, we certainly hope to have some rain, given the haze condition now in Singapore. The Member asked two supplementary questions. Let me reiterate the principle first before I address the two questions. I would like to reiterate what I just said in my reply. Humanitarian concern itself is not prohibited. We should separate the cause from the content and the conduct. That is the core principle behind the licensing framework and the classification framework. 
The line is crossed when conduct or content undermines public order, national security or stability, or where foreigners use Singapore as a platform to further political causes.
[+2 sentences] Given that principle, I hope that Members can also understand that any assessment has to be contextual, because that is the prevailing assessment of the agencies and the regulator, at a point in time. As I shared earlier, we have provided approvals for performances.
For example, on 16 May 2026, an event called "To The Unforgotten", a variety event, classified R18, some mature content.
[+1 sentence] The event was meant as a celebration of humanity and solidarity with various groups around the world.
It featured a song, poem and multimedia on the Israel-Gaza conflict. And we have another example, it was a play, "6 Microlectures on Genocides".
[+1 sentence] They had multiple stagings, the latest staging in May last year, also classified R18, with mature themes.
The play comprised short works that explore themes of genocide, war crimes and contemporary conflicts. And another example is a stand-up comedy tour called "Namaste", a couple of years ago in September 2024, classified Advisory 16, some mature content and coarse language, and contained a segment where the comedian spoke about the Israel-Gaza conflict.
[+9 sentences] So, having material and content on causes itself is not prohibited. The licensing framework is designed to protect young people from unwanted content but allow people to make decisions on what they can watch. But at the same time, having some boundaries on the kind of content that may stir up public disorder or national security considerations. That is the approach that we have taken and we will continue to be principled on that. In terms of the processes, it is really a point that I had made earlier, assessments are very contextual. I encourage applicants to engage the agency, IMDA, early. And IMDA will also engage relevant agencies if their inputs are needed. The earlier that the applicants engage IMDA, the earlier conversations can start, and the earlier we can give clarity and guidance on the kind of content that may be approved and the kind of content that we may have some concerns over. So, clarity and guidance can be provided, but I encourage applicants to reach out to IMDA early.

[+1 sentence]Mr Speaker, the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) closely monitors developments in the online landscape and tracks emerging safety risks for young users, including those highlighted by the Member.
To do so, IMDA draws on a range of sources, including public feedback, industry engagements, market data and developments in other jurisdictions.
[+3 sentences] Like many commercial digital products, apps and social media services come and go. We therefore focus our regulatory efforts on types of online communication services that have become widely used in Singapore and where safety risks have been clearly flagged. These include social media services and app stores.
Under the Broadcasting Act, IMDA may direct a social media service or app store to disable Singapore users' access to egregious content, such as content that advocates or instructs on suicide or self-harm. A social media service with significant reach or impact in Singapore may also be required to comply with the Code of Practice for Online Safety – Social Media Services. IMDA considers various factors as laid out in the Broadcasting Act, including the extent and nature of the effect that the service has on people and communities in Singapore.

The first part is what is already available now, and what the Ministry for Digital Development and Information is doing. I want to highlight the fact that today, we already have some safeguards in place that would protect our young from inappropriate content or harmful content, and things that they may not be appropriate for their age.

Submarine cable disruptions and Singapore connectivity

Most submarine cable disruptions worldwide come from accidental fishing and anchoring damage, but Singapore's connectivity stays resilient through diverse connections.

covers this turn's highlighted sentences · summary of Surveillance and Monitoring of Mechanisms Installed under "Guiding Principles for Underwater Infrastructure Defence Exchanges"
Globally, most submarine cable disruptions result from accidental damage caused by fishing and anchoring activities. Industry data indicates about 100 to 200 such incidents occurring worldwide each year. Singapore's international connectivity has nevertheless remained resilient due to the diversity and volume of our connections to other countries.
[+3 sentences]  International cooperation is essential because submarine cables span multiple jurisdictions and issues can be transboundary. For example, the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) has information-sharing arrangements with partner governments and industry stakeholders to monitor submarine cable systems. Operators must also promptly notify IMDA of cable incidents affecting their systems, and repair cable cuts and restore affected services expeditiously.

Digital Connectivity Blueprint and cable operator obligations

The 2023 Digital Connectivity Blueprint aims to double submarine cable landings in 10 years, with operators required to monitor, report and repair faults.

covers 5 highlighted sentences in 2 sections · also: GUIDE agreement on underwater infrastructure security
[+9 sentences]Sir, I thank the Member Dr Neo for his two supplementary questions. Let me just take a step back to provide more some context to this matter. Firstly, I agree with Dr Neo that international connectivity through submarine cables is critical. It is important for our digital economy and very important for many aspects of the industry and our daily lives even. Every time we download something or we talked about social media, what my colleague Ms Rahayu spoke about, requires data to flow and data flows across the world through submarine cables primarily. Our approach has been two-fold. One, is to enhance resilience through diversity and connectivity because we cannot control whether the cables will be cut in which part of the world. The cables are transboundary, they go through different jurisdictions and we cannot control things outside our jurisdiction. So, first and foremost, to minimise disruption, we are building up diversity of our submarine cables that come through Singapore and interconnect one another and build up the volume, so that if one cable is cut somewhere in the world, cable operators have the option of diverting traffic to other options that they have.
Through the Digital Connectivity Blueprint that we launched in 2023, we had indicated that Singapore is committed to provide landing space and resources to enable submarine cable landings to double within the next 10 years.
[+3 sentences] From 2023, the next 10 years. So, building up the diversity and resilience. That is the first point.
The second is that we also work closely with the industry and we require cable operators to monitor cables for faults, report them within an hour of detection and ensure speedy repairs. That is one of the obligations that we have placed on our cable operators, even though some of the cuts may be outside our territorial waters, but those obligations still apply on our cable operators.
[+4 sentences] Thirdly, we are working with like-minded countries, for example, in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), IMDA chairs the ASEAN Working Group of Submarine Cables, and is a member of the International Advisory Body for Submarine Cable Resilience. Both platforms seek to strengthen cooperation on submarine cable protection, resilience and repair, as well as promote information sharing and exchange of best practices. We had a fuller reply in January this year on our cooperation with neighbouring countries.  That is important, because I mentioned earlier the cable cuts, may, most of the time, happen outside our jurisdiction and we have to work very closely with all like-minded parties and it is a shared outcome, a mutual interest that we will work on.
Lastly, on the point of GUIDE, I just to add on that GUIDE brings countries which agree on shared principles and potential areas of defence, where defence establishments could collaborate on enhancing the security of critical underwater infrastructure. It has been signed by 17 countries, including Singapore, and we will continue to work closely with countries that have expressed interest to sign up.

Government efforts against investment scams

The Government has stepped up measures against scams involving self-effected transfers, including investment scams, through messaging platform requirements, bank cooling periods and public education.

covers this turn's highlighted sentences · summary of Adapting Shared Responsibility Principles Framework to Authorised-transfer Scams
[+1 sentence]Mr Speaker, the number of scam cases and amounts lost have decreased in 2025 and in the first half of 2026.
Nevertheless, scams are still a concern and as noted by the Member, investment scams recorded the highest losses among all scam types.  The Government has stepped up efforts to combat scams involving self-effected transfers, including investment scams. For example, online messaging platforms will be required to implement measures that make it more difficult for unknown contacts to engage users without the end-users' consent, and to display warnings alerting users to the potential scam risks posed by such contacts. Major retail banks have progressively implemented cooling periods for higher-risk activities, such as adding of payees, raising of transaction limits and making large transfers that result in draining of accounts, to give consumers an opportunity to re-consider whether the transfer they intend to make is legitimate. The Government will also continue to drive public education efforts to help the public better protect themselves against investment scams and make more informed financial decisions.
[+1 sentence] Sir, the Shared Responsibility Framework (SRF) focuses on phishing scams involving unauthorised transactions.
It is not suitable for scams involving self-effected transfers.
[+3 sentences] Defeating such scams requires all parties to exercise vigilance: the messaging platforms to make it more difficult for scammers to engage victims; and the banks putting in place cognitive breaks to give time for victims to reconsider.  And importantly, individuals can take practical steps to protect themselves and approach every investment opportunity with care and caution. For example, please check whether it is indeed a Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)-regulated financial institution offering the investment product and contact the financial institution directly through its official contact channels.

Whatever countermeasures we put in place, the scammers will find new ways of trying to break through these safeguards. So, we have to continuously review our systems and to be vigilant.
The Bill that was passed yesterday, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) Bill that deals with countermeasures against scams would also help, I think, to strengthen the deterrence against scammers and also to enhance the protection for consumers.
[+8 sentences] Sir, I would also like to just briefly mention that in this regard, the bad guys that we are dealing with here are the scammers. Therefore, we should really point the attention of our deterrence measures and our penalties towards this group of individuals – the scammers. The financial institutions (FIs) are our partners. We work closely with them and in fact, I want to take this opportunity to express our appreciation to the FIs and, in particular, the many employees working in the FIs who are a very key part of this overall defence against scams. Members would have read reports from the media about how some of the staff in our FIs have been on their guard and sometimes, taking measures to try and protect consumers, at the risk of being scolded sometimes by the consumers, because they will block what they think are suspicious transactions and the consumers are not happy. They would vent their frustrations toward the staff, but the staff helped to prevent some of these scams from happening. Afterwards, of course, the consumers are appreciative. But during that time when they were trying to get the transaction through, there was some unhappiness.
I think it is important to recognise this: that the FIs and the staff working in the FIs are trying their best to work together with us to try and reduce the risk of scams. I must also add that the FIs have also leaned forward to try and help on a discretionary basis to provide goodwill payment. That means this is not part of the SRF. This is what they do on their own – goodwill payment – on a case-by-case basis, based on the financial situation of the victims, especially those who come from more vulnerable backgrounds.
[+1 sentence] The banks, the FIs will try to do more to help them.

Unauthorised banking transaction dispute resolution

MAS is asked how it ensures dispute processes for unauthorised banking transactions are accessible and fair, and whether banks should bear more proof burden.

covers this turn's highlighted sentences · summary of Ensuring Fair and Accessible Dispute Resolution Processes for Unauthorised Banking Transactions for Consumers Without Legal or Financial Expertise
[+1 sentence]Mr Speaker, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) requires banks to provide clear channels for customers to report unauthorised transactions and to handle such disputes in a fair manner.
This includes promptly commencing investigations and pending the outcome, not requiring customers to pay for the disputed transaction and its related charges. Banks are expected to clearly explain to customers how liability has been assessed.
[+1 sentence]  Payment card schemes also have established rules to protect customers.
Customers who promptly raise disputes with their card issuers will generally not be liable for unauthorised transactions with merchants that do not enable the 3-D Secure (3DS) protocol. Instead, the merchant involved will be liable for the loss.  If customers were assessed to be responsible for the loss following investigations, banks may offer goodwill payments to customers taking into account the circumstances of each case, including the customer's financial situation and whether they come from vulnerable backgrounds.
[+1 sentence]  Sir, where customers disagree with a bank's assessment on liability, they can escalate the matter to the Financial Industry Disputes Resolution Centre which offers an independent and affordable avenue for dispute resolution without the need for legal representation.

[+1 sentence]Ms Phua.

[+13 sentences]I thank the Minister for the answer, and I do agree that the Ministry of Home Affairs Bill yesterday was of great help and that FIs are indeed our partners. Especially that they do lean forward to our residents who are especially vulnerable. But I just want to read an extract from a resident of mine who has no access to pro bono services because he is not poor enough or low-income enough, and this is what he said: "When I became a victim of fraud. I naively assumed that the facts would speak for themselves. I did not authorise the transactions, did not click on any phishing links, did not disclose any OTPs, and reported the matter immediately upon discovering the fraud. I thought that would be enough. Instead, I discovered that an ordinary consumer is expected to navigate a very complex web of banking regulations, contractual terms and legal arguments simply to protect their rights." He said, "Throughout this process, I have had to review pages of submissions and banking documents, understand banking regulations and liability frameworks, interpret terms and conditions, prepare legal and factual submissions, and respond to arguments made by large financial institutions with access to legal compliance and fraud specialists. I subsequently realised that I had failed to raise potentially significant arguments during adjudication, simply because I did not know enough to appreciate their relevance at the time." This has led my resident to ask how many ordinary Singaporeans who do not qualify for pro bono legal services, how many of them would realistically be able to defend themselves? Is our system stacked against the ordinary consumer without legal aid? I feel for this and I also know what the Government is doing. So, I just want to hear the Ministry's comments on this and how we can maybe improve the situation.

covers this turn's highlighted sentences · summary of Ensuring Fair and Accessible Dispute Resolution Processes for Unauthorised Banking Transactions for Consumers Without Legal or Financial Expertise
[+7 sentences]Mr Speaker. I understand what Ms Denise Phua is saying, because there are indeed a range of different types of cases. Some instances, the individual involved may be partially responsible for what happened because they did not take enough care, they did not do enough to protect themselves. They, in fact, sometimes proactively participate in some of these, thinking that they were able to make an investment, and later on it turned out to be the wrong decision. But in some cases, and as Ms Phua shared, it is somebody who is genuinely being scammed and the person did not authorise the transaction. And that is why I think the system, to be fair to all stakeholders, need to have a rigorous process to assess the facts of each case before deciding what is the response. So, I hope Ms Phua will agree with me that the rigour in the system is actually a good thing, because that is what we can then do to help the genuine cases even more, while not opening up in a way a floodgate and encouraging the wrong types of behaviours and moral hazard in the system – because then that will mean we have less resources available to help the genuine cases.
That is the first point I want to make about the rigour of the process. But the second one is I want to assure Ms Phua is this, and I mentioned it in my main reply, that we do not design a system whereby the individual would need to receive legal assistance on a pro bono basis to be able to help represent himself or herself, because this is where the Financial Industry Disputes Resolution Centre comes in. Through this centre, it will offer an independent and affordable avenue for dispute resolution without the individual involved having to get legal representation. So, this is one way in which we can provide some assurance to individuals who are caught and have a genuine case for dispute resolution.

[+1 sentence]Sir, Singapore adopts a risk-based, multi-layered approach to identify travellers who may intend to engage in unlawful activities, including vice.
The Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) leverages data analytics to conduct pre-arrival risk assessments using advance passenger information, intelligence, watchlists and other available information to identify travellers of interest or other factors, such as patterns of travel, that may warrant further scrutiny. Travellers arriving at our checkpoints who are assessed or profiled to present a higher risk will also be subjected to further interviews and checks, before ICA determines whether to grant them entry.
[+1 sentence]  ICA continually reviews and strengthens its border security capabilities to address evolving threats, including those posed by transnational vice syndicates.
In January this year, ICA introduced a new upstream measure by issuing No-Boarding Directive (NBD) notices to airlines operators at Changi and Seletar Airports, which requires the operators to prevent persons identified as prohibited or undesirable travellers from boarding flights bound for Singapore.
[+1 sentence] NBD notices may be used across a range of cases involving identified prohibited or undesirable persons, including those who are engaged in vice-related activities.

[+1 sentence]Sir, I thank Ms Diana Pang for the question.
Foreigners seeking entry into Singapore and who are assessed to have the intention to engage in vice-related activities in Singapore will be deemed as undesirable persons. Having said that, the ICA does not track those foreigners who are on visa-free entry and who are engaging in illegal activities in Singapore.
[+1 sentence] Nevertheless, with traveller assessments now extended further upstream during pre-arrival, checks have become more robust.
In 2025, approximately about 45,000 foreign visitors were refused entry at Singapore's checkpoints. This represents about a 38.3% increase from around 33,000 foreign visitors who were denied entry in 2024. These foreigners were assessed to pose immigration or security risks, or believed to have the intention to come to Singapore to work illegally.

[+1 sentence]Mr Speaker, Singapore does not condone the use of forced labour.

Singapore-registered or headquartered companies are also expected to comply with the laws and regulations of the jurisdictions that they operate in.
[+2 sentences] Forced labour in supply chains is a transnational issue. Effective enforcement against such practices would require international cooperation.

[+2 sentences]Thank you, Mr Speaker. The three supplementary questions by the Member are linked, so I will take them together.
First, as I mentioned in my main reply, we do not condone the use of forced labour in Singapore, and our legislation prohibit this and these are our national legislation here. We do not have extraterritoriality in relation to these regulations. However, we inform Singapore-based companies that operate overseas that they need to comply with the laws of the jurisdictions that they operate in.

Mr Jeffrey Siow128 words
[+7 sentences]As at 31 March 2026, the estimated liabilities of the Pioneer Generation (PG) Fund exceed its balance by about $0.9 billion. This shortfall is attributable to two factors. First, healthcare costs and MediShield Life premiums have risen faster than expected, and these account for the main shortfall. Second, scheme enhancements, such as CareShield Life Additional Participation Incentives, have contributed to the shortfall marginally. The PG Fund is designed to support long-term commitments and outlays that will materialise over many years. Its estimated liabilities will change over time, and we do not seek to match the Fund balance exactly to these liabilities at any one point. But the Government will make fund top-ups as needed and ensure that the commitments made to our seniors remain fully funded over time.

Mr Ong Ye Kung197 words
[+9 sentences]There are existing mechanisms in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to enhance our collective capabilities to detect and respond to emerging infectious diseases. For example, the ASEAN Emergency Operations Centre Network and the ASEAN Biological Threats Surveillance Centre (ABVC) are platforms that enable ASEAN member states to share communicable disease intelligence. Disease surveillance information shared to the ABVC is published on an online dashboard that is updated daily. Our National Public Health Laboratory also maintains longstanding collaborative ties with their counterparts in ASEAN member states, facilitating information exchange, sharing of technical experience, sharing of reference biological materials and confirmatory testing. ASEAN is in the process of establishing the ASEAN Centre for Public Health Emergencies and Emerging Diseases (ACPHEED). Once established, ACPHEED will play a central role in coordinating regional communicable disease surveillance efforts. Notwithstanding the above, a pandemic crisis is a global and not a regional event. Global efforts to conduct disease surveillance, genome sequence high risk and novel pathogens, notify and share them promptly with the world, are essential to effective pandemic preparedness and response. The key platform today is the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data, which Singapore is actively involved in.

Role of Peer and Community Support Networks in Mental Well-being and Strengthening Lower-barrier Avenues Complementing Formal Mental Health Services› Written Answers to Questions2 turns · 287w · 0 highlighted
written-answer-24752
Dr Choo Pei Ling63 words

Mr Ong Ye Kung224 words
[+11 sentences]Peer, community and informal support networks are an important part of Singapore's mental health ecosystem. Family members, friends, colleagues, peers and community volunteers are often the first to notice when someone is struggling. They can provide emotional support, encourage early help-seeking and, where appropriate, offer initial support while guiding individuals to suitable services. Many individuals may not be ready to seek professional help immediately. To provide lower-barrier avenues of support, the Ministry of Health has established First Stop for Mental Health services, including the national mindline 1771 and mindline.sg. These services allow individuals to seek information, guidance and support, including anonymously if they prefer. Where needed, they also encourage individuals to seek formal mental health services and facilitate referrals with the individual's consent. Beyond these services, we are strengthening community capability through efforts to improve mental health literacy, reduce stigma and equipping more people with basic mental health skills. These include programmes, such as the Health Promotion Board's Peer Support Training Programme and the Agency for Integrated Care's online Mental Health Awareness modules. These efforts complement, rather than replace, formal mental health services. Together, they support earlier identification of concerns, encourage timely help-seeking and ensure that individuals receive the level of care that best meets their needs, from community and peer support for those with milder concerns, to professional assessment and treatment where required.

Mr Ong Ye Kung184 words
[+9 sentences]The Ministry neither tracks medication returned by patients nor disposal costs of such items in public healthcare institutions. However, there are measures in place to help reduce medication wastage. Firstly, public healthcare institutions generally supply patients with sufficient medication to last until their next appointment and do not provide excess medication. For newly prescribed medications, a shorter duration may be dispensed initially and subsequently refilled if there are no side effects. Secondly, together with patients or their caregivers, pharmacists will review the prescribed medication regime including adherence to medication, at relevant transition points of care to identify medications that are no longer required and minimise unnecessary wastage. As excess medication is not routinely dispensed, returned medications are more commonly due to patients passing on. Lastly, public education efforts play an important role in reducing medication wastage. The Pharmaceutical Society of Singapore conducts outreach and public education activities to encourage patients not to over-collect medications. Complementing these efforts, the Ministry of Health "Know Your Meds" Series educates patients on how to keep track of their medication supplies and avoid overstocking which might result in wastage.

Protecting Against Unauthorised AI-generated Likeness in Advertisements and Operationalising Online Safety Commission's Mandate over Inauthentic Material Abuse› Written Answers to Questions2 turns · 319w · 0 highlighted
written-answer-24766
Mr Yip Hon Weng59 words
[+1 sentence]asked the Minister for Digital Development and Information in light of paid advertisements using AI-generated likenesses and voices without consent (a) whether platforms will be required to verify advertisers and obtain consent attestations before publication; (b) whether persistent disclosure and expedited removal will be mandated; and (c) when the Online Safety Commission's powers over inauthentic material abuse will commence.
Mrs Josephine Teo260 words
[+12 sentences]The Advertising Standards Authority of Singapore (ASAS) adopts a consistent approach in considering whether advertising content is acceptable, regardless of whether artificial intelligence (AI) is used. Under the Singapore Code of Advertising Practice (SCAP), advertisers are responsible for ensuring that their content is legal, decent, honest and truthful. Advertisers should disclose AI use where necessary to avoid misleading consumers. They should not portray a person or their property without consent and ensure all endorsements or testimonials are genuine. ASAS adopts a complaints-based approach in reviewing potential advertising breaches and can get advertisers to amend or withdraw non-compliant advertisements. Beyond SCAP, the Government also issued new and enhanced Codes of Practice under the Online Criminal Harms Act on 17 August 2026 to strengthen safeguards against online advertisements that impersonate individuals. Designated online services are required to verify advertisers' identities and prevent and promptly remove the publication of suspected scam advertisements. The Online Safety Commission (OSC) provides relief to victims of online harms under the Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act (OSRAA). This currently covers the most prevalent and severe harms, namely intimate image abuse, image-based child abuse, doxxing, online harassment and online stalking. OSC can act on online material generated using AI and that meets the thresholds for these five harms. Inauthentic material abuse is one of the further categories of online harm under OSRAA that will be progressively implemented, as the OSC builds its capabilities in a sustainable and scalable way. We will provide more details on the commencement of this online harm for relief under OSRAA in due course.

Government and Commercial Data Compromised in LiteLLM Supply Chain Attack and Measures to Prevent Recurrence› Written Answers to Questions2 turns · 256w · 0 highlighted

Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song58 words

Mrs Josephine Teo198 words
[+12 sentences]LiteLLM is widely used open-source artificial intelligence (AI) software. Hackers compromised it by using login details stolen in an earlier breach to add malicious code to software updates. GovTech used scanning and detection tools to identify the affected Government agencies and informed them quickly. The attack was confirmed to have compromised only one user account, which supported a small number of agencies. The affected agencies changed any login details that might have been exposed and checked their system records for signs of unauthorised activity. There is no evidence that any Government data, including personal data held by the Government, was stolen or compromised. The Government does not have a complete picture of how the incident affected commercial entities. Each company should check its own systems, fix any problems and make any required reports. The Singapore Cyber Emergency Response Team has published an advisory on the incident and can provide cybersecurity guidance and help where needed. Attacks on software supply chains are an ongoing threat. The risks cannot be removed completely. However, the Government will keep reviewing and improving how it prevents, detects and responds to such attacks, so that similar incidents are less likely and cause less harm.

[+12 sentences]This question was addressed by the reply to Questions No 81 to 82 for oral response during the Parliament Sitting on 10 September 2026. [Please refer to ​"Shared Facilities Available for Deep Tech Startups and Ventures", Official Report, 10 September 2026, Vol 96, Issue 37, Written Answers to Questions for Oral Answer not Answered by End of Question Time section.] The Government is committed to fostering a pro-innovation environment that enables businesses, including deep tech startups and small and medium enterprises (SMEs), to support research and development (R&D) and deployment of emerging technologies. The Government does work closely with our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) and research institutes to provide startups and SMEs with access to shared R&D facilities, equipment and technical expertise. Key initiatives include the Centres of Innovation established in partnership with the IHLs and platforms operated by the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), such as Innovation Factory@Singapore Institute of Manufacturing Technology. Specialised facilities are also available, such as Biosafety Level 2 (BSL-2) and Class 100 compliant laboratories through the National Graduate Research Innovation Programme (GRIP) Labs, advanced cleanroom infrastructure and industry-grade tools through national platforms, such as the National Semiconductor Translation and Innovation Centre (NSTIC) and the National Quantum Federated Foundry (NQFF), as well as shared life sciences, chemistry and engineering facilities through A*STAR's A*StartCentral. Companies can also use the A*STAR Scientific Equipment and Services Finder (A*SEF) to identify and access more than 1,500 scientific equipment and related services across A*STAR. For regulatory sandboxes, the Government's approach is to design sector-specific frameworks that are tailored to the needs of each industry, as the risks, stakeholders and regulatory considerations differ significantly across industries. A single national sandbox policy may not adequately account for these differences. Several agencies already operate sandboxes tailored to their respective sectors. For example, the Energy Market Authority has introduced a regulatory sandbox for energy innovations, including novel business models in the electricity sector. In the digital and technology space, the Infocomm Media Development Authority has supported experimentation through initiatives, such as the GenAI Sandbox, which allows enterprises to trial generative AI solutions before wider adoption. The Government will continue to assess the needs of emerging technologies and industries and, where appropriate, establish shared R&D facilities and regulatory sandboxes to support technology development, testing and adoption.
