Ms Jasmin Lau221 words
[+9 sentences]The Skills and Workforce Development Agency (SWDA) oversees employment, career and skills support for jobseekers and works with partner organisations, including the National Trades Union Congress' Employment and Employability Institute, to provide career matching services. Most jobseekers who receive employment support through SWDA and its partners secure new jobs within a year. We recognise that a prolonged job search can be discouraging. For jobseekers who require more time or support, career coaches will work with them to review their career goals, identify viable career pathways, broaden their job search and assess relevant training needs. Beyond career coaching, jobseekers can tap on a broad range of placement and training programmes to strengthen their employability and transition into new roles. These include Career Conversion Programmes (CCPs) and the SkillsFuture Career Transition Programme (SCTP), which support jobseekers to reskill or upskill for new job opportunities. Employers hiring long-term unemployed Singaporeans through CCPs receive enhanced salary support of up to 90%, while long-term unemployed Singaporeans who participate in SCTP receive up to 95% subsidy on their course fees. The Government will continue to strengthen employment, career and skills support, with the formation of SWDA as an important step to bring together employment facilitation and skills development capabilities. This will enable more coordinated, personalised and targeted support for jobseekers, including those who undergo longer job searches.

Mr Chee Hong Tat206 words
[+10 sentences]The Housing and Development Board (HDB) works closely with the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) on fire safety matters for coffee shops within HDB blocks. Before commencing renovations, coffee shop operators are required to engage a qualified person and submit their fire safety plans to SCDF for approval, as well as their renovation drawings to HDB for approval. Before occupation is allowed, the operator must obtain a Fire Safety Certificate from SCDF. After operations have commenced, HDB conducts annual fire safety inspections and advises operators on good fire safety practices. Operators are also required to submit kitchen exhaust system servicing reports when renewing their tenancy or outdoor refreshment area licence. This ensures that kitchen exhaust ducts are properly maintained and cleaned, reducing the risk of grease build-up that can cause fires to spread. These checks are in addition to SCDF's scheduled and unannounced inspections of these premises. On fire insurance, owners of privately-owned HDB shops are required under the terms of their lease with HDB to purchase basic fire insurance. Tenants of shops let out by HDB are required to take up fire insurance for HDB's fixtures and fittings, and public liability insurance of at least $1,000,000. Non-compliance may result in non-renewal or termination of tenancy.

[+6 sentences]At the inception of the Pioneer Generation (PG) Fund in 2014, $8 billion was set aside based on estimated funds required to fulfil the commitment to PG seniors. As of 31 March 2026, the PG Fund had an estimated liability of $5.75 billion, compared with a balance of $4.84 billion. The difference has arisen mainly because healthcare costs and MediShield Life premiums have increased faster than expected. There have also been enhancements to the support provided to PG seniors, including the CareShield Life Additional Participation Incentives, which have added modestly to the Fund’s liabilities. The Government closely monitors the Fund's balance, estimated liabilities and utilisation trends to ensure the sufficiency of the Fund. We do not seek to keep each Fund's balance exactly matched to its estimated liabilities at any point, but will make top-ups as needed taking into account the size of any estimated shortfall and the overall fiscal position to ensure that we meet the commitments made to our seniors.
Differences by Firm Size on Ability to Accommodate TG-FWAR Requests and Main Operational Barriers Faced by SMEs› Written Answers to Questions for Oral Answer Not Answered by End of Question Time2 turns · 271w · 0 highlighted

Ms Jasmin Lau209 words
[+9 sentences]The Tripartite Guidelines on Flexible Work Arrangement Requests (TG-FWAR) took effect in December 2024. It sets out the process for employees to make formal requests for flexible work arrangements (FWAs), and for employers to consider these requests on business grounds. The Ministry of Manpower (MOM) does not mandate the reporting of FWA requests, so as not to impose significant compliance costs on businesses. As such, MOM does not have data on the small and medium enterprises' (SMEs') ability to accommodate FWA requests.  However, MOM's survey of firms found that SMEs were less likely than non-SMEs to offer FWAs. In 2025, nearly seven in 10 SMEs had offered at least one type of scheduled FWA, compared to around eight in 10 non-SMEs. Common operational constraints faced by SMEs include leaner staffing and limited scope to redistribute work when employees request flexibility to take on different work hours or a reduced load. SMEs can tap on the SkillsFuture Workforce Development Grant (Job Redesign+) to redesign jobs to better manage their staffing needs, and the Productivity Solutions Grant to offset the costs of purchasing information technology (IT) solutions that enable more dynamic and flexible manpower scheduling. Tripartite partners will continue to monitor and support employers in accommodating FWA requests from their employees.
Thresholds for Justifying a Permanent New School and Lead Time to First Primary 1 Intake› Written Answers to Questions for Oral Answer Not Answered by End of Question Time2 turns · 269w · 0 highlighted
written-answer-na-24670
Ms Gho Sze Kee64 words
[+1 sentence]asked the Minister for Education (a) what demand and capacity thresholds the Ministry uses to determine when a new primary school is required in an area, including the projected size of the primary-school-age population and duration of demand needed to justify a permanent new school; and (b) what is the typical lead time from identifying the need to the school's first Primary 1 intake.
Mr Desmond Lee205 words
[+9 sentences]The Ministry of Education (MOE) regularly reviews the demand and supply of primary school places at both the national and local levels. In doing so, we consider factors including the current and projected number of school-going children, planned housing developments, capacity in nearby schools and accessibility for residents. As circumstances differ across areas, we do not just apply a single population threshold or fixed duration of demand. Instead, we assess each case holistically, including the local context and projected longer-term demand. A new school requires substantial investment, and must have sufficient students over time to support a good range of educational programmes and co-curricular activities. We would therefore build one when we project that there will be a sustained demand that cannot be adequately met by nearby schools. Apart from building new schools, MOE may expand the capacity in existing schools where possible, to address short-term increase in demand in an area. From identifying the need for a new school to its opening, time is required for planning and design, construction, staff recruitment and pre-opening preparations. We generally do our projections and announce new school several years in advance of the first Primary 1 intake, to give parents and residents clarity on future school provision.

Ms Jasmin Lau189 words
[+8 sentences]In the past four quarters, the number of retrenchments in Singapore's e-commerce and tech-enabled sectors fluctuated within the range of 480 to 580, below the peaks observed in 2023 and 2024. Retrenchments were driven largely by business reorganisation or restructuring. The six-months re-entry rate among retrenched residents within these sectors improved, from 53% in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 61% in the first quarter of 2026. The Skills and Workforce Development Agency (SWDA) offers a suite of programmes to support retrenched workers to re-enter employment. In particular, jobseekers who require significant reskilling can participate in career conversion programmes (CCPs), the Mid-Career Pathways Programme (MCPP) and the SkillsFuture Career Transition Programmes (SCTP). For example, the CCPs provide employers with up to 90% salary support to train mid-career career switchers who may not have the full set of skills required to take up new roles immediately. SWDA also works closely with sector agencies and industry to refresh the jobs and opportunities offered through these programmes. Companies undertaking regional retrenchments that affect Singapore-based employees are required to declare the support provided to affected workers as part of the Mandatory Retrenchment Notification.

[+7 sentences]The Government recognises the diverse caregiving needs of working Singaporeans, including those caring for elderly parents or dependants with disabilities. [+6 sentences]The vaccination coverage for the diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis (DTaP), Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), and polio vaccines have been consistently high. [+8 sentences]School-based interventions are a key part of our efforts to address vaping. The referrals to Health Sciences Authority (HSA) reflect the vigilance of schools and the institutes of higher learning (IHLs) in detecting vaping-related offences and their close coordination with HSA. Referral numbers alone are therefore not used as a measure of the effectiveness of school-based deterrence measures. We have stepped up our measures to address vaping among youths since September last year through a multi-pronged approach of prevention, enforcement and rehabilitation. On prevention, the Health Promotion Board (HPB) works closely with the Ministry of Education and HSA to educate youths on the harms of vaping, strengthen their ability to resist peer pressure and reinforce anti-vaping messages through the school curriculum, orientation programmes and peer-led initiatives. For youths caught vaping, they are subject to HSA enforcement actions as well as disciplinary measures by their schools and IHLs. These are complemented by counselling and intervention programmes to address underlying causes and support behavioural changes. Those who need help to quit vaping can contact HPB's QuitLine for cessation support, and resources are available to help parents speak to their children about vaping.

Extent to Which School-based Assessments Award Marks for Students' Responses that Demonstrate Correct Conceptual Understanding› Written Answers to Questions for Oral Answer Not Answered by End of Question Time2 turns · 266w · 0 highlighted
written-answer-na-24845
Mr Yip Hon Weng60 words
[+1 sentence]asked the Minister for Education (a) how does the Ministry verify that school-based assessments award marks for responses demonstrating correct conceptual understanding even when they differ from expected answers; (b) how marking errors involving valid alternative answers are identified through moderation or appeals; and (c) whether common review standards will be introduced to distinguish conceptual errors from merely non-standard reasoning.
Mr Desmond Lee206 words
[+9 sentences]School-based assessment is an integral part of teaching and learning. Its primary purpose is formative – to help teachers understand how well students are learning, give feedback and provide learning support. In marking tests, teachers award marks for valid responses even if the responses differ from model answers. When there are questions on how a response has been marked, such as when students review the marked scripts, schools have processes to review the marking and adjust the marks awarded, if necessary. Where a higher level of consistency in marking is required, such as in school-based examinations, schools have additional measures, including a standardisation process where teachers come together to review the marking criteria and mark sample scripts to standardise their marking approaches. Should teachers come across valid responses that have not been anticipated, the marking criteria will be adjusted to recognise these responses. The setting and marking of school-based assessment is managed at the school level, in keeping with the formative purpose and lower-stake nature of such assessments. The Ministry of Education provides professional development and guidance to schools to deepen teachers' assessment literacy and build a shared understanding of marking principles and practices. We will continue to support and guide schools in strengthening assessment practices.

Every FAJT performs both teaching and non-teaching duties, which may include form teachership, co-curricular activity duties or other responsibilities in the school. FAJTs are paid hourly for the work performed and their working hours are subject to a cap. Guidelines for Institutes of Higher Learning on Use of AI-writing Detection Tools› Written Answers to Questions for Oral Answer Not Answered by End of Question Time2 turns · 307w · 0 highlighted

Mr Desmond Lee248 words
[+11 sentences]This response also addresses questions filed by Ms Lee Hui Ying and Ms Cassandra Lee on this topic. [Please refer to "Review of AI Detection Tools and Academic Policies at Institutes of Higher Learning and Establishment of Transparent Student Appeals Process", Official Report, 8 September 2026, Vol 96, Issue 35, Written Answers to Questions section.] All the institutions of higher learning (IHLs) have policies governing the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in assessment and academic work. These are aligned with the Ministry of Education's guidance that AI use should support learning and that guardrails are in place to uphold academic integrity so that assessment outcomes reflect the effort and intended mastery by students. IHLs clearly inform students whether and how AI may be used, as requirements may vary across assessments and assignments. They also have established processes for students to appeal assessment and disciplinary outcomes, including in cases of suspected unauthorised AI use. Students are given an opportunity to respond to any allegation or concern before disciplinary action is taken. IHLs assess whether AI detection tools add value to their broader assessment and academic integrity frameworks. Where such tools are used, detection scores alone do not determine academic misconduct. In cases of suspected misconduct, educators exercise professional judgement by reviewing the student's work and establishing the facts through appropriate follow-up. This includes engaging the student and where necessary, requesting evidence of the learning process, such as drafts or earlier work. Educators remain responsible for the final grading decision.

Mr Desmond Lee116 words
[+5 sentences]The Ministry of Education (MOE) commissioned studies on adolescents’ sleep in 2021. These studies showed that adolescents' sleep duration and bedtime patterns are associated with a range of individual and environmental factors, including age and pre-bedtime activities, such as leisure use of electronic devices, that is, social media and gaming), studying or doing homework, and chatting or texting. International research shows that inadequate sleep can impair adolescents' cognitive functioning, such as sustained attention, working memory and mood. Adequate sleep is therefore important for students' learning, well-being and physical development. Under the Grow Well SG initiative, MOE will continue to partner relevant agencies, parents and the community to promote healthy sleep habits and support students' overall well-being.

Mr Chee Hong Tat117 words
[+4 sentences]For public sector development projects, the National Parks Board (NParks) works with agencies to retain mature trees where feasible, unless the trees cannot be integrated or transplanted, or pose a risk to public safety. For example, the Home Support Programme will be rolled out later this year to help PwDs build the skills to live independently in their own homes.

[+8 sentences]The Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) does not track statistics specifically on young children found unsupervised in public places who were assessed as being in need of care or protection. Where Police suspect that such cases may involve neglect, they would refer them to MSF for investigation. From 2022 to 2024, there was an average of 539 child neglect cases that required statutory intervention. When a child is found to be at risk due to neglect, MSF's immediate priority is to ensure the child's safety. Where the child can remain safely at home, MSF, a Child Protection Specialist Centre or a Family Service Centre will first implement safety plans, monitor compliance and work with the family to improve parenting practices to ensure adequate care and safety of the child. Where there is sufficient evidence that a parent or caregiver may have committed an offence, the case may be referred to the Police and prosecution may be considered.

Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat66 words
[+1 sentence]asked the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (a) why work permit holders may be employed in coffee shops and food courts but not in NEA hawker centres, given all are cooked-food trades; (b) how many Long-Term Visit Pass (LTVP) and Long-Term Visit Pass Plus (LTVP+) holders work as hawker stall assistants as at 1 September 2026; and (c) whether the venue-based distinction will be reviewed.
Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien170 words
[+7 sentences]Hawker centres are a unique part of Singapore's cultural heritage and it is important to preserve the local identity and heritage of our hawker culture. Only Singaporean Citizens and Permanent Residents are allowed to be stallholders at our hawker centres, and stallholders are required to physically operate their stalls. This is unlike other licensed food shops, which may be managed by commercial entities that hire employees to run their outlets. Nonetheless, stallholders in hawker centres can hire eligible Long-Term Visit Pass (LTVP) and Long-Term Visit Pass-Plus (LTVP+) holders, who are already part of the Singapore family nexus, to work as stall assistants. This strikes a balance between supporting stallholders' manpower needs and the preservation of hawker centres' local identity. As of 1 August 2026, there are about 300 LTVP and LTVP+ holders working as stall assistants in cooked food stalls in hawker centres. We will continue to monitor the situation and review our policies where necessary, to strike a balance between manpower needs and the Singaporean identity of hawker centres.

Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien89 words
[+4 sentences]Over the last three years, Singapore imported an average of 560,000 tonnes of fibre per year, comprising fresh vegetables and related produce. Pre-identification of Vulnerable Residents Unable to Evacuate Independently in a Fire, and Opt-in Protocol for Providing Such Information to Responders during Emergencies› Written Answers to Questions for Oral Answer Not Answered by End of Question Time2 turns · 329w · 0 highlighted
written-answer-na-24890
Mr Yip Hon Weng61 words
[+1 sentence]asked the Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs following fatal HDB fires involving seniors (a) whether SCDF can identify beforehand residents who are unable to detect a fire, call 995 or evacuate independently; (b) if not, why not; and (c) whether an opt-in protocol making such information available to responders during emergencies will be piloted.
Mr K Shanmugam268 words
[+13 sentences]As fire incidents are dynamic and can evolve rapidly, the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) responders will need to assess conditions on site to prioritise individuals requiring rescue or evacuation. Where evacuation is necessary, SCDF prioritises residents on the affected floor and those living two floors above. Pre-maintained information on residents requiring assistance during fire incidents may not be the most updated and will need to be verified on site.  The Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats are designed as a stand-alone fire compartment to limit fire spread prior to SCDF's arrival. In addition, home fire alarm devices (HFADs) are mandatory in all new homes since 2018. For existing HDB flats, HFADs are mandated for homes carrying out fire safety related addition and alteration works. All homeowners are encouraged to install HFADs, as early warning can be critical in allowing occupants more time to respond, evacuate safely and call for assistance.  Seniors and residents with mobility impairments who are unable to evacuate independently should remain in their units, move to a safe room, close the door, call 995 and provide their location and await assistance. This approach is aligned with international best practices and reduces the risk of injury during evacuation. Those who are deaf, hard-of-hearing or otherwise unable to call 995 may contact SCDF by SMS at 70995.  The community also plays an important role in supporting vulnerable seniors during emergencies. SCDF works with the People's Association's Community Emergency and Engagement Committees to regularly organise block evacuation exercises. These exercises help residents better understand their neighbours' needs and support those who may require assistance during an emergency.
Strengthening Awareness on National Security Threats and Attracting Talent through ISD Junior College and Polytechnic Scholarship› Written Answers to Questions for Oral Answer Not Answered by End of Question Time2 turns · 342w · 0 highlighted
written-answer-na-24892
Mr Lee Hong Chuang69 words
[+1 sentence]asked the Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs (a) how will the Ministry assess whether the Internal Security Department (ISD) Junior College and Polytechnic Scholarship strengthens youths' awareness of national security threats and interest in national security related careers; and (b) whether similar scholarships or exposure programmes by other public agencies will be encouraged, where appropriate, to build early awareness and attract talent.
Mr K Shanmugam273 words
[+10 sentences]The Internal Security Department (ISD) Junior College (JC) and Polytechnic Scholarship is part of ISD's ongoing initiatives to strengthen public awareness of Singapore’s internal security threats. These initiatives include partnering agencies through the SGSecure movement, community partners, such as the Religious Rehabilitation Group, and the Ministry of Education, to increase greater awareness among the general public and students, about the threats posed by terrorism, violent extremism and radicalisation. The JC and Polytechnic Scholarship is a new initiative to deepen awareness amongst our youths of our internal security threats and introduce pre-tertiary students to career opportunities with ISD. Launched in August 2025, the initiative attracted 231 applications. Ten students from various JCs and polytechnics were selected for the inaugural award in early 2026. In addition to a $2,500 cash prize, the recipients participated in a two-day immersion programme at ISD, where they gained deeper insights into ISD's work, including opportunities to engage with ISD officers. Participants shared that the Immersion Programme had deepened their understanding of ISD's work and internal security threats facing Singapore. They also expressed greater interest in a career with ISD, describing its work as deeply fulfilling and meaningful, contributing to the protection of Singapore's national security. The ISD JC and Polytechnic Scholarship complements similar efforts across the Home Team Departments to engage students early and raise awareness of the Ministry of Home Affairs' work and career opportunities, through a range of initiatives, including book prizes, internships, learning journeys, work attachments and job-shadowing opportunities for pre-tertiary and tertiary students. We will continue to consider other opportunities for early engagement, taking into account the nature of each Department's work and talent needs.
Stepping Up of Surveillance and Enforcement Actions against Online Investment Scams› Written Answers to Questions for Oral Answer Not Answered by End of Question Time2 turns · 337w · 0 highlighted
written-answer-na-24894
Mr Liang Eng Hwa71 words
[+1 sentence]asked the Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs in view of the $170 million in investment scam losses in the first half of 2026 (a) whether MAS and the Police will step up surveillance and enforcement action against online investment scams; and (b) whether MAS and the Police will work with social media and messaging platforms to detect scam groups masquerading as investment learning communities.
Mr K Shanmugam266 words
[+8 sentences]In investment scam cases, scammers may approach victims using accounts not previously known to the victim to offer lucrative investment products. To address this, under the new Code of Practice for Online Messaging and Conferencing Services (COP) issued in August 2026, designated online messaging platforms must implement measures to alert users to potential scam risks posed by unknown contacts and require user consent before the user can be added into a chatgroup by an unknown contact.  The new and enhanced COPs for Social Media Services and e-Commerce Services also require the designated online services to disallow the publication of advertisements offering financial services or products to Singapore users, unless the advertiser is licensed by any Singapore authority or authorised by a licensed entity to do so in Singapore.  In addition, the Police work closely with online platforms to disrupt investment scam content, including those by scam groups masquerading as investment learning communities. When there is reasonable suspicion that the content is preparatory to or in furtherance of the commission of scams, the Police may issue Directions under the Online Criminal Harms Act to online service providers to restrict Singapore users' access to such content. The Monetary Authority of Singapore has worked with major retail banks to prevent scammers from profiting from investment scams by introducing additional friction for high value transfers. For example, banks have progressively implemented cooling periods for adding of payees, raising of transaction limits, and making large transfers that result in draining of accounts. This gives consumers an opportunity to re-consider their transfers or investments if they suspect that it is a scam.

Regulation and Assessment of MOE Kindergartens and Kindergarten Care Centres› Written Answers to Questions for Oral Answer Not Answered by End of Question Time3 turns · 390w · 0 highlighted
written-answer-na-24898
Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan67 words
[+1 sentence]asked the Minister for Education (a) whether Kindergarten Care (KCare) centres in MOE Kindergartens (MKs) are licensed under the Early Childhood Development Centres Act; (b) if not, what standards govern staff qualifications, staff-child ratio and children's safety and well-being while in KCare; and (c) whether and how the KCare component is separately specified and evaluated when Student Care Centre operators for schools co-located with MKs are appointed.
Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan54 words
[+1 sentence]asked the Minister for Education (a) whether MOE Kindergartens (MKs) are assessed against the Early Childhood Development Centres Regulations 2018 and the Early Childhood Development Centres Code of Practice; (b) if so, by whom and how often; and (c) how many MKs have been assessed and how many required rectifications in the past decade.
Mr Desmond Lee269 words
[+13 sentences]My response will address the questions raised by Ms Eileen Chong on regulations and standards for MOE Kindergartens (MKs) and Kindergarten Care. MOE Kindergartens are directly operated by the Ministry of Education (MOE) and are part of the primary schools they are located in. MKs are regulated under the Education Act, and are excluded from the Early Childhood Development Centres (ECDC) Act. MOE has put in place oversight structures and processes to ensure adherence to quality and safety standards in all schools, including MKs. All MKs also take reference from the ECDC Regulatory Standards prior to commencing operations. MKs conduct a yearly self-appraisal and undergo regular validation exercises by MOE that take reference from the Singapore Preschool Accreditation Framework under ECDA. MOE headquarters follows up to provide consultation and relevant support where needed. Kindergarten Care (KCare) centres are operated by student care centre (SCC)-KCare operators. These operators are selected by considering how well the KCare component meets MOE's guidelines on staff qualifications and training, staff-to-child ratios, as well as programme implementation, environment setup and standard operating procedures to safeguard children's safety, health and well-being. Pre-operations checks are conducted to ensure each KCare centre meets baseline standards before commencing operations. To ensure that KCare centres are held to standards comparable to those required by ECDA on similar childcare services, MOE has put in place a KCare Quality Assurance Framework that takes reference from ECDA's Code of Practice for kindergarten-level childcare services. MOE conducts regular appraisals to ensure standards are maintained. We will continue to work closely with ECDA in ensuring that our MKs provide quality preschool education for our children.

Shared Facilities Available for Deep Tech Startups and Ventures› Written Answers to Questions for Oral Answer Not Answered by End of Question Time3 turns · 430w · 0 highlighted
written-answer-na-24902
Dr Neo Kok Beng70 words
[+1 sentence]asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) (a) to the Government's knowledge, how many shared facilities, inclusive of equipment for research and development, are available for deep tech startups and ventures; and (b) whether the Ministry or relevant agencies will consider setting up shared facilities in emerging areas, such as quantum and space technology, and life sciences, such as clean room and Good Clinical Practice (GCP) laboratories.
Dr Neo Kok Beng34 words
[+1 sentence]asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) whether the Government will consider implementing a national sandbox policy for emerging technologies or industries, where current legal or regulatory measures are not available.
Dr Tan See Leng326 words
[+11 sentences]The Government is committed to fostering a pro-innovation environment that enables businesses, including deep tech startups and small and medium enterprises (SMEs), to support research and development (R&D) and deployment of emerging technologies. The Government does work closely with our institutes of higher learning (IHLs) and research institutes to provide startups and SMEs with access to shared R&D facilities, equipment and technical expertise. Key initiatives include the centres of innovation established in partnership with the IHLs, and platforms operated by the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), such as Innovation Factory@Singapore Institute of Manufacturing Technology. Specialised facilities are also available, such as Biosafety Level 2 (BSL-2) and Class 100 compliant laboratories through the National Graduate Research Innovation Programme (GRIP) Labs, advanced cleanroom infrastructure and industry-grade tools through national platforms, such as the National Semiconductor Translation and Innovation Centre (NSTIC) and the National Quantum Federated Foundry (NQFF), as well as shared life sciences, chemistry and engineering facilities through A*STAR’s A*StartCentral. Companies can also use the A*STAR Scientific Equipment and Services Finder (A*SEF) to identify and access more than 1,500 scientific equipment and related services across A*STAR. For regulatory sandboxes, the Government's approach is to design sector-specific frameworks that are tailored to the needs of each industry, as the risks, stakeholders and regulatory considerations differ significantly across industries. A single national sandbox policy may not adequately account for these differences. Several agencies already operate sandboxes tailored to their respective sectors. For example, the Energy Market Authority (EMA) has introduced a regulatory sandbox for energy innovations, including novel business models in the electricity sector. In the digital and technology space, the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) has supported experimentation through initiatives, such as the GenAI Sandbox, which allows enterprises to trial generative artificial intelligence solutions before wider adoption. The Government will continue to assess the needs of emerging technologies and industries, and where appropriate, establish shared R&D facilities and regulatory sandboxes to support technology development, testing and adoption.
